Moreover, the legislation to be submitted to the committee-I have received notice for a sitting this afternoon at three o'clock-is most contentious and of a dangerous nature. It is the open door to communism through international labour organizations.
Those who enjoy trips to Geneva, to New York and to labour conventions anywhere else in the world may find it wonderful. But there are communists who belong to and who control labour organizations in France and other countries. They will mix with our people.
Sugar

The fact that labour organizations are becoming more internationalized than ever is a menace to Canada and to the whole world. Some labour leaders think highly of international organizations. I believe in the right of labour men to unite; but I do not see why labour men should be controlled by outsiders, by foreigners, who implant communism in such international organizations, with the purpose of domination of all labour men by communism.
I stand against that; I protest against it. This is a warning. maintopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO SUPPLY-INCREASE IN RATE OF RATION

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO SUPPLY-INCREASE IN RATE OF RATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in response to requests made in this house recently I should like to make a statement on our sugar supply situation. Hon. members will recall that in my statement to the house on March 12th I said that the world sugar supply had been improving and that probable supplies available to Canada would be of the order of somewhere between 80 and 87 pounds per capita refined basis. That statement was made before any of the main sugar crops had been harvested. As a result of unusually fortunate climatic conditions the output of sugar from the current Cuban crop has considerably exceeded expectations, and instead of the estimated 5J million ' tons, it seems likely to reach almost 6i million tons. The international emergency. food council has, therefore, been able to increase its allocations to participating countries. Canada's share of this increase is 22,000 tons of raw sugar. After adjustment for year-end carry-overs our total allocation for 1947 has been set at 626.000 tons.
Sugar supplies however must be thought of as a continuing flow and we have, therefore, had to give careful thought to the prospects for 1948. In this connection we have had the benefit of consultation with our British and American colleagues and with other experts in the sugar trade. Our conclusion is that we cannot expect, and should not count upon a
[Mr- Pouliot.]
recurrence in 1948 of the phenomenal 1947 Cuban crop. The balance of probabilities is that the 1948 Cuban crop will be a good crop in comparison with normal, but could easily run one million tons below this year.
World production of sugar in the year ended August 31, 1946, was about 3J million tons below 1939 production. During the year ending August 31, 1947, world production should approximately equal the last pre-war year; but over a long period of years world sugar consumption has increased on an average by more than half a million tons per annum, so that under normal conditions world production would still be about 5 million tons short of demand. However, lack of purchasing power in Europe and Asia and the situation with regard to dollar exchange may very well reduce effective demand in these areas. Against this there are no invisible supplies in the western hemisphere and it remains to be seen what effect decontrol of sugar in the United States may have. It may be a year from now before this can be accurately judged.
At the time of my previous statement on March 12 it was anticipated that there would be an increase in Canadian production of beet sugar. It now appears that on account of abnormal weather conditions we may look for some reduction.
The conclusion we have reached is that while 1947 probable supplies seem likely to make possible the distribution of some seven or eight additional pounds of sugar per capita during the balance of this year, it would be prudent in the light of all conditions to plan for a greater than normal carry-over into 1948. The consumer's sugar ration for 1917 was increased by three pounds on April 1 and in effect by a further three pounds on June 9 through the de-rationing of jams, jellies, marmalade and honey. We now propose another increase of three or four pounds during the second half of this year. Two additional coupons will be declared valid in August and one or two late in November. At the same time we shall advance the industrial ration by ten points in each industrial category, which will put the basic industrial quota at ninety per cent of 1941 usage. Since the third quarter industrial quotas have already been distributed, the additional ten per cent will go forward as a supplementary quota during the latter half of July.
As hon. members know, the United States terminated its household sugar ration two weeks ago but has retained in full force its industrial ration. Our considered view is that we Should not follow that example in Canada. The main purpose, indeed I might say the

Questions
sole purpose of rationing is to ensure fair distribution at fair prices to all sections of the country and to all classes of consumers, whether household or industrial. Canada is a country of very great distances and in many sections is characterized by a rather thinly scattered population. Large industrial users of sugar are chiefly concentrated in a few areas. If sugar were de-rationed, ordinary business judgment might well lead most of these large industrial users to stock up heavily and such heavy restocking could absorb very large quantities of sugar, which in turn would almost certainly lead to disorderly distribution, and spotty shortages creating acute local embarrassment in many parts of the dominion. Our system of rationing is such that we cannot de-ration one class of consumer without opening up large gaps and loopholes in the system which would rapidly undermine it.
Our conclusion is that it is in the general interest, and particularly in the interest of householders and small businesses, that sugar rationing should be retained in full force at least until the 1948 supply prospects are clear, but at the same time to increase the rate of ration as rapidly as circumstances permit.

Mr. Speaker, I desire to put on the record a matter which normally I think I should have brought up on the motion to go into supply, but I still think I am within the rules in bringing it up on the second reading of an interim supply bill. I shall not elaborate on the points to which I shall refer; I want to leave them with the members of the house and of the government for their consideration not only during the rest of the present session but also during the recess; because these points deal with the whole question of how in my opinion we should handle the public business in parliament in the future.
This has nothing to do with party matters, and I would ask every member of my own party as well as every other member of the house to feel free to criticize the suggestions I am putting on the record. I shall do no more than enumerate them now, because this is not the time to make a speech on the various matters with which they deal. These are my suggested improvements in parliamentary facilities and procedure:

I do so because these communications support very well my contention that the neglect of the needs of our pioneers and older citizens is a long established tradition in this country.
Let me read from a copy of the letter written by David Thompson in February, 1844 in which he outlines the statement of his circumstances and his distressed condition. He addressed the following letter to the governor general's secretary:
Sir,
Various circumstances, but principally an attack of the influenza of which I am recovered, have hitherto prevented my acknowledging the honour of the receipt of your letter of the 22nd ultimo wherein "His Excellency regrets that X should be placed in the unfortunate position I describe." Permit me to remark, something of an unusual train of circumstances has led to this state. In last May, when I informed His Excellency that I was about to proceed to Washington to dispose of my maps of the northwest countries, and Oregon territory, to the executive of the United States; His Excellency was pleased to claim the first offer of them to Her Majesty's government, to which I acceded. Had I proceeded to Washington and there sold my maps, and the information I possess on those countries, I should have been in a very different state from what I am at present. The last summer was given to the maps of the Oregon territory for Her Majesty's foreign office; the result of my labours, His Excellency informed me, was thanks without reward. When His Excellency was in Montreal, I had the honour of mentioning to him the maps of the boundary between Canada and the United 'States by the treaty of Lord Ashburton; he was pleased to say, "the maps are valuable and I wish to have them;" but candidly added, I cannot give an order for them until the money is voted by the legislature.
The members of the assembly to whom I mentioned this, all said, that for maps so necessary for the secretary's office, the sum required by His Excellency placed in the estimates will directly pass. I accordingly made the maps and sent ,them to Kingston, but His Excellency had no means at his disposal to recompense me. Thus passed my time from May to late in December without affording me the means of supporting my family, to do which, has obliged me to sell all that can be sold. Around every government there is a class of persons who have more or less passed their lives in its services, and thereby become dependent on it. His Excellency has been pleased to allow that my long services give me some claim on government, yet how very different is my neglected situation from many others; as many notice, among other instances, that of Mr. Borne, who for the sale of his seat in the House of Assembly for Rimouski, to Mr. Robert Baldwin received the handsome reeom-
[Mr. Herridge.l
pense of two hundred pounds per annum to take charge of the Chambly canal, for which his habits of life never qualified him.
I have the honour to be,
-	Sir,
Your obedient servant,
David Thompson.
That letter was written over one hundred years ago, yet how indicative it is today of present conditions! While deputy ministers have their salaries increased, while the same is true of boards of transport commissioners, the old age pensioners of the country are asked to live on an inadequate income. Let me now read the brief letter which forms the reply sent by the secretary of the governor general; Sir,
In reply to your letter of the 27th ultimo I am desired by the governor general to inform you that there are no funds at his disposal from which you can be remunerated for the time and labour you have bestowed upon the maps to which you refer.
As Her Majesty's government do not require these maps, there cannot be any objection to your endeavouring to dispose of them to the executive of the United States, which you appear to have the same chance of effecting as at the time you offered them to His Majesty's government.
His Excellency regrets the state of distress to which you describe yourself to be reduced, and would willingly relieve you from it, if it were in his power, but there are no funds available.
As I say, that was over one hundred years ago. How applicable it is today. That great man, who served Canada so well, whose skill and energy and work are only now receiving widespread recognition, died in his eighty-seventh year, and just a few days before his death he entered in his diary the following words: "This day I borrowed two and sixpence from a friend. Thank God for that relief." On February 10, 1857, [DOT] he died and he now lies buried in an unmarked grave in Mount Royal cemetery, Montreal. I have outlined these circumstances because they represent a tradition which has grown up in the country of overlooking our pioneers and aged citizens.
I am one of the younger pioneers of the district in which I live. I was not born there, but I have lived there since my boyhood, and all through the years I have witnessed the same sort of treatment meted out to these people who have built up the country. I remember playing with the Indians as a boy. The band of Arrow Lake Indians consisted of twenty-five persons at that time. When the white man first arrived in the Kootenay area, the Indian population numbered several hundred, but in 1906 that number had been reduced to twenty-five and today we have an Indian population of one. I mention that because I believe hon. members of this house, particularly the C.C.F. group, believe that old age pensions should be paid to Indians. If measures of that kind had been taken years ago we would not have the tragedy of the dying out of an Indian band in that area.
As a boy I knew many pioneers and old-timers, and I delight to recall those olden days and to relive in my mind the scenes I saw. I had the opportunity of knowing a man who took part in the first discovery of gold on the mainland of British Columbia, out at the junction of the Columbia and the Pend-d'Oreille rivers. I refer to Nels Demers, a French Canadian who came from somewhere in the Ottawa valley just prior to the discovery of gold. He worked for years prospecting, timber cruising and assisting in government surveys. He devoted his whole life to the benefit of that area. I remember as a boy being asked to attend in his cabin when he was dying. I might say that in that period I remember Conservative speakers representing the provincial government telling audiences that old age pensions must be brought in. I think at that time certain European countries were held1 up as examples. Audiences were told that old age pensions would be brought in by the Conservative government of the day; that is, the provincial government. I remember the late Sir Richard McBride saying of the district in which I live: "Viewing as I do the great natural resources of this area, I cannot conceive of anything but increasing prosperity so long as labour is applied to these great resources". In the same speech I remember his referring to the plight of some of these older people who were living in log cabins along this lake throughout my constituency, whose later days were largely provided for by the generosity of friends and acquaintances, many of whom were unable to afford the amounts they gave for these purposes. I remember this one man in particular, Nels Demers, after whom a community is named to this day. He was a French Canadian who rendered great service to this country. He died in poverty because it was the tradition of the country, and is today, not to make adequate provision for our pioneers. I remember some of the first builders of the steamboats in the district from which I come, men who assisted in packing the machinery over the mountains, bringing pistons, boilers 83166-295
and things of that type on horse packs; men who built under the most difficult circumstances the wooden hulls of the craft that sailed on that lake.
I remember too the men who built the steamers which carried men from the United States for the gold rush, and later carried freight. I remember these older men very well. I remember a number of them particularly who after a lifetime of work on boats and steamships on the Columbia river were largely maintained by the generosity of their friends and neighbours, and ended their days in poverty. I remember something of the first lumbermen and loggers. I remember the building of some of the first mills and the bringing to the district of several hundred young French Canadians. I remember some of the older men who built the mills and did the logging in the very early days and made it possible to build the early cities and the early communities. I think of two men in particular, who were expert woodsmen, good millwrights, good all-round craftsmen. They worked unceasingly until they were over seventy-five years of age. I refer to a man named Miles Carrol, after whom a community on the lake is named, and another man known as Andy. I remember those two men passing their later days in poverty, supported by their friends and acquaintances.
I remember some of the early trappers and prospectors who went through what today would be considered untold hardships in packing through supplies to the distant traplines and distant prospects. I knew a man by the name of Dad McBain who gave up his traplines only after he was eighty years of age. He earned his living as long as he could; after he was eighty years of age he had to be maintained by the generosity of his friends and acquaintances. I know, too, of the plight of some of the early farmers in the district and some of the first war veterans, men who went to the South African war, and some of the early workers in industry, particularly in the smelters, in the latter part of the last century and the early part of this one. While I recognize that there are some improvements and some benefits, I maintain that in this bill we are carrying forward the Canadian tradition of not supplying the needs of our pioneers and aged people according to the resources of this country.
I am not going to repeat in detail the many valid criticisms made by hon. members with regard to this bill, or to present their arguments. I think that is unnecessary. Anyone reading Hansard can see again and again the sound and valid arguments put forward by members of all parties. In the observations

Old Age Pensions

I have to offer I do not for one moment criticize the provincial or other officials who throughout the years have been administering the Old Age Pensions Act. I have had some experience with old age pensioners, because I am in a sense an old-timer in that district. I tried to do what I could for hundreds of these old people, assisting them to fill in their forms and meet the requirements of the law. I must say in all fairness that I have found the officials most cooperative and most desirous of doing all they could for the old age pensioners according to the regulations and according to the circumstances. I know a good number of these officials. In fact I think it would be difficult to find an official administering the old age pensions provincially who is not looking forward to the day when the means test will be abolished.
I think the amount provided for in this bill is too low. I do not think there is any argument as to that; I shall not go into the legal arguments but will just give a concrete illustration or two. I know an old miner. He is close to ninety. He has worked for years in the mines and in the smelters of this country. Picture the position of a man who under present provision for old age pensioners in British Columbia-which is one of the highest in Canada-has to pay out of that pittance $15 a month for a single room; and that is quite reasonable under the present circumstances. I said to him, "How do you live on the amount of the pension?" He said, "I have a slice of toast and a cup of coffee for breakfast. Sometimes I get a friend to give me lunch, but I really aim at having one good feed a day in the evening. No one can justify the amount we are allowing these people under those circumstances.
Then I come to the rural dwellers, those who live in country places. I will say that in many instances they are in a better position. I know of dozens of men who have a shanty in a small town or country place, or out in the backwoods; they live under somewhat better conditions. It is possible for them to make the dollars go a little farther. Usually they do not have house rent to pay. They build log cabins or frame shacks. They carry water from a nearby spring, and they cut their own wood. One of those men showed me his budget recently. I am not going into details, but I can say that he is a man of seventy-eight years whose shack is neat. He keeps accounts, and in those accounts he had totalled his budget for the month of March. In the budget he had entered amounts for groceries, and the necessary items of clothing, including shirts and socks. Then he had bought small quantities of tobacco, and

there were no expenditures for other types of recreation, with I believe the possible exception of a weekly newspaper. His budget showed expenditures of $40.41, despite the fact that he was living with as much care as he could.
How can anyone say that the amount for which this legislation provides is sufficient for either urban or rural dwellers? I support the contention of those who say the means test should be abolished. It is one of the most unpopular tests with all those who work in the old age pensions branch. I have had many officials tell me of the great difficulty it presents to them, and the many cases of unfairness which have come to their attention.
I could give one or two illustrations. I have in mind an old gentleman in my home village of Nakusp of possibly 450 people. He was the first permanent white resident of that village. He had come down from Revelstoke on a raft years ago. That man is nearing eighty today, and for a period during the war he received the old age pension. Later in the war, because of a shortage of labour, he was persuaded by the people in the district to help out by doing a little extra work. He is a good craftsman, particularly as a shoemaker and carpenter, and a general handyman. For three or four months he earned at the rate of about $25 a month. What was the result? That old pioneer's pension was cut off. At that age he continued to earn his living, without reapplying for pension.
That is a state of affairs which should not exist in this country. I know of difficulties with which some of the old soldiers and old veterans who could not qualify under the War Veterans Allowance Act have been faced. These are men who possibly served in the imperial army. They may have seen service in the South African war or in the first world war. They may have built up some small competence in the form of homes or small ranches. But they hesitate to sign papers applying for pension because they want that property to go to their children. Upon their decease they do not want to have the pensions deducted from their estates.
I know of a farmer, a pioneer in my district, who came from the old country many years ago. He has built up a fine orchard and has been producing apples over a period of years. Now he is too old to work much and because of the difficulty of obtaining labour the operation of his orchard has become a problem. He does not wish bo sell the orchard, but wishes it to go to his grandson. If however that man were to accept a pension, a lien would be placed against the orchard. The result has been that he has not taken the

Old Age Pensions
pension. Today that old gentleman, who has spent large sums of money in this country, who has been a good citizen, who has cleared acres of land and planted a large orchard from which he has produced trainloads of apples and other fruits, is now in the position where he must live on what little he can make. All this is brought about because he does not wish to apply for an old age pension owing to the means test provisions.
I believe the qualifying age is too high. Today we find many old soldiers who cannot qualify for war veterans allowance, and who are prevented from getting old age pension. In this class we find many former miners and lumberjacks, men who have been working in wet mines, or under mountain conditions in the woods. Many of these men, because of the conditions under which they have worked, are prematurely aged. They are not fit to work in the mines or in the woods after sixty years of age, or at the very most after sixty-five years, and yet they are not able to obtain old age pensions. The same applies to some of the earlier industrial workers, those who have worked in the smelters and saw mills of the district.
Many of these men have lost their strength and their health. They are deprived of old age pensions until they are seventy years of age. I might point out that to some extent this situation has been recognized in British Columbia. The people of that province recognize that in this modern industrial society there are many people who have to be cared for before they reach the age of seventy years. In British Columbia we have what is known as the Social Assistance Act, which makes it possible for every citizen of the province, regardless of age, to receive amounts somewhat the same as those paid under the old age pensions scheme, or probably a little less.	They may receive these payments
whether their destitute condition is caused by economic handicaps, invalidism or other types of handicaps.
British Columbia has shown the way in this respect. And the fact that it is being done in that province is evidence that this legislation is insufficient when it does not permit a person to receive an old age pension until the age of seventy years has been reached.
There have been placed before the house many sound reasons, on humanitarian and economic grounds, for amendments to the bill. I support, as do the majority of the people I represent, an increase of the pension to at least $50 a month, the removal of this obnoxious means test and the lowering of the 83166-295}
qualifying age. Those proposals have the support of a great majority of the Canadian people.	[DOT]
When the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) suggested that hon. members were criticizing the bill on political or electoral grounds he was absolutely wrong. Members of the house, regardless of the party to which they belong, who criticized the deficiencies in the bill, are truly representing the people they have been sent here to represent. I support the proposal put forward by the hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) that after second reading the bill be sent to a committee for examination. I believe that is a good suggestion, one of the many good suggestions the hon. member has placed before the house in this and in preceding sessions.
This bill is of great importance to a wide section of the Canadian people, and particularly to those who are in need of old age pensions. I am not one who believes one can get something for nothing, but I think the bill should be sent to a committee where it would be possible to examine officers of the Department of National Revenue. I do not hold the de luxe ideas of finance or taxation which are held by the hon. member for Edmonton East (Mr. Ashby). I do not believe that the people who accept the same philosophy of life as I do would hold to that theory of taxation. But we do believe that if presented with the facts, the people of Canada are willing to pay an amount of money sufficient to enable these old people to live on an adequate scale.
I listened with interest to the constructive speech delivered by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton). I thought last night he delivered a most informative speech, and before concluding what I have to say may I point out that I was particularly impressed by his point that what we can do for these senior citizens of Canada can be more than something of a financial nature. I was interested in his point that this government and the provincial governments must be increasingly concerned about the welfare of these people in other respects, so that they may have an opportunity, not just quietly to live out the rest of their days in a well-fed and warm condition, but to be active participants in the life of their communities.
This is not a partisan question. I believe there is no subject in Canada at this time less partisan that that of making proper provision for our senior citizens. I do urge that the government give consideration to the wishes and views of the great majority of the people
Old Ago Pensions

of Canada who desire to see these people properly cared for. We boast of our natural resources, our wealth and our position in the united nations. We boast about our position in world affairs. But we must support that boast. We read the story of the past; we read the history of Egypt, Greece, Rome, the Latin countries and Great Britain. We read our own history. Any country which fails to provide adequately for its senior citizens finally goes into decay and oblivion. I believe that without unnecessary strain we can give these people sufficient with which to live lives of happiness and contentment.
In conclusion I just want to say to the minister that the bill presented to this house is no credit to our past, and holds out little hope for the future.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to take part in this debate for a number of reasons, all of which I do not intend to mention at this time. I represent a constituency in which there are a great number of elderly people. In the city of Victoria and on the southern end of Vancouver island we probably have more elderly people in proportion to the population than any other part of Canada. That is due to two reasons. When people are born on the southern end of Vancouver island, or come there, apparently they live longer than they would anywhere else. Next, it has without doubt the best climate in Canada, and elderly people like to come there, and they are welcomed when they come, so that they may live the rest of their lives in comparative comfort. I believe that their numbers will increase as the days go by. All the beautiful and comfortable spots are not in my riding; many of them are in the riding of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) who can enjoy the sunshine on the southern point of the island.
There is another reason for my speaking today. There has been a tendency in this house to ignore some of the real considerations and consequences of old age pensions-and I place some emphasis on the word "consequences". It is easy for an hon. member to rise in this house and expound the advantages of pensions. That is as it should be, and I am the last one to say that it should not be done. I think I have as much sympathy as anyone for elderly people, here or elsewhere.
There has been a tendency during this debate to pick numbers or amounts out of the air and argue the value of a certain amount per month to be given to old age pensioners. These people are encouraged to believe that

the country can and will provide more than it is possible to provide. For that reason I think it is bad for anyone to go beyond what he believes this country can reasonably carry out.
My main reason for speaking is that I thought that by using some of the facilities of the department with which I am fairly closely associated I could obtain figures which would be of interest and which would prove a guide to those who wanted to give real consideration to the problem before us. I have prepared a table showing the costs of about nine different proposals which have been made since the opening of the house and during this debate. Along with that table I am going to place on the record the number of people over seventy years of age, the number over sixty-five and the number over sixty years. Then anyone who wants to really find out what his scheme will cost can do so by simple multiplication.
This would apply only when there is to be no means test. There are many things that we could not find out when there is to be a means test, but with the figures I am giving a fairly accurate estimate of any scheme can be obtained provided there is no means test. Before giving this statement I should like to refer briefly to a statement made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) when he was replying to the minister who is piloting this bill through the house. He said, as reported on page 4290 of Hansard:
He has told us of the great plan that was put forward two years ago, a plan which the government voluntarily brought forward, declaring it would undertake to pay $200,000,000. And now he tells us that the proposals which are now before us will cost this nation only $20,000,000. He says that it is a great step forward. I suggest that if it is a great step forward it is a very short one. The government has laboured and brought forth a mouse.
The hon. member has probably had a lot of experience in bringing up mice with long tails, but I want to state to the house that in one instance he told the whole story while in another he told only part of it. He did not tell the house that the $20,000,000 was extra to the $70,000,000 odd which we are paying already. The total of those two amounts comes quite close to the $100,000,000 mark. He did not tell the house that the $200,000,000 offer is still there. So far as I know the government has not reneged in any way on its proposals to the dominion-provincial conference, and I am quite confident that the government will not renege on this or any other promise.
There is another thing which the hon. member did not tell the house, something which has not been mentioned here. Because of the increased exemptions provided by this bill,

Old Age Pensions
60,000	more people will receive these benefits than were receiving them in 1947. Surely that point is well worth stating. I suppose it was not in his interest at the moment to say anything about that. Nor did he tell you- probably he did not know-that the leader of the opposition rose almost immediately after the minister had resumed his seat and made his statement at once. If I were doing it that quickly there are a lot of things I would forget too, and that puts a different light upon it.
These figures I think are interesting. Six-sevenths of all the aged people who are receiving pensions under this scheme are receiving the full pension. Only one-seventh of these people have any deductions whatever made from their pensions. So the means test surely does not mean quite as much as some hon. gentlemen would lead us to believe in this debate.
I am supporting this bill, and I think I should give some reasons why I am supporting it.
Let me say first that I wish it were possible for us to divide our thinking into two classes. We have with us the men and women who are over seventy years of age, and we have also those who will be approaching that age in later years. For myself I cannot go back seventy years, but I can go back for quite some time. I can go back to the days when these men were working on our farms, probably five and six months out of the year, at $20 a month, and when they left the farm they would go to the logging camps and there get about the same amount of pay. I know because I have been there myself. I got the magnificent sum of $14 a month for the privilege of going to work in the dark and coming home in the dark, and of having pork and beans to eat almost three times a day, and for dessert dried apples and prunes; and going home quite fat on it all, and with lots of company.
These are the same men who worked in industry, when our industries were humble concerns and the men did not get full employment. Nevertheless if it had not been for their efforts we would not have had our industries today. These were the men who cut down our forests and turned our fields into the productive areas of today. They were the men who built our railroads and other public services on short time and on short pay. The big wages of today have not always been paid. It is only comparatively recently that men have been receiving big wages, since Henry Ford, whether he was right or wrong, raised the wages of every man in his employ by one dollar a day. That was the start of
our high wages. But those who are now seventy receive no such wage. These men have laboured long and diligently, and if a few of them have misspent their money I for one am quite prepared to forgive that, remembering the things they have done for us.
I wish we were in a position to segregate that group of men who have done so much for us from those who today are in an entirely different position. They are getting wages which enable them to set something by. They are putting money by in insurance and in annuities and in victory bonds, and if we do not take away from them the incentive to save, they will continue to save. My hon. friend here (Mr. Reid) says that some call that old-fashioned doctrine today. It is because of the old-fashioned doctrine and independence of these people that we are today standing in our places and giving them the praise we are giving them. But if we did what some suggest we should do in this bill we should rob these people, or those who come after them, of their independence and their initiative and their incentive to save. That is one reason why I do not want these fancy ideas. We can go too far in both directions. But there is a balance on which we can travel that is right.
We cannot raise the amount of money that some people suggest we should raise for old age pensions without adding more burdens to the small taxpayers who find it difficult even today to pay the taxes on their small incomes. Let us wait a while and see if we cannot get the exemption raised. Let us wait a year or two and see if we cannot catch up with our obligations to the veterans-and our bill for them this year is $430,000,000 or $440,000,000. Let us see if we cannot get some of these things cleared out of the way and then look again at the old age pension. Or at the worst, according to the minister, all we have to do is to wait for the completion of agreements with the two larger provinces, and then this $200,000,000 proposal would go into effect.
There is another reason why I am supporting this bill. I have studied and worked on this question longer, I think, than most members. I tried back in 1917, 1918 and 1919 to work out with our own group a pension superannuation plan. I have been studying it and figuring on it for quite a long time. The first speech I made in this house was on compulsory contributory old age pensions-or old age superannuation, as I prefer to call it. I was alone that year. In 1940 an hon. member was elected for Nanaimo who gave considerable support to that plan. Also in the same year the member for Edmonton East gave some
Old Age Pensions

support to the idea. But it died down. There was nothing much said about it until recently, and now it looks as if there is a possibility of getting old age superannuation going. But how are we going to do it? If you build the old age pension up to $50 a month, will those pensioners be anxious to separate themselves from five or six or seven per cent of their income-to provide what? What have they in the United States? There they get $29 and some cents a month. Are they going to part with a percentage of their income to get what some hon. members propose, a pension of $50 a month?
I will close this part of my remarks with this further statement, that we cannot have all the security we want in every respect. We cannot spend $250 million-$260 million it is this year-on family allowances, $430 million for veterans and $100 million for unemployment insurance. In other words two-fifths of all that we expect to collect this year will go in social security work. I contend that we must divide our money and decide where we are to place it. Are we to place it all on one thing, or on another? So far as I am concerned I want to see some day better hospitalization, at least cheaper if not free. I should like to see cheaper medicine and more doctors' help, because I think there is a preventive for the man who reaches seventy and has not sufficient money. You help him so that he does not get into the position of needing assistance from anybody, and I think that is much better for us all. Let us look at the thing calmly. Let us not put all our eggs in one basket. I feel quite sure that we will not. In our family allowances I believe that we went up to the rail as close as we dare go. I am not advocating going back on things, but I do say this: in whatever we have to do at the present time let us do it in a rational, practical and reasoned-out way.
I know Mr. Speaker, that you have ruled that the reading of speeches is not permitted. I have not been reading mine so far; probably it would have been better for the house if I had. I should like the privilege of reading for a little while because what I have to say now is pretty well filled up with figures, and unless they are right they do not mean anything at all.
Consideration of the various proposals listed on the tables I have before me gives a good picture of the increased cost of the alternatives as suggested in the house, and also how these costs will increase in the coming years due to the growth in population of people over sixty-five years of age. At the same time the population forecasts indicate that the number of persons over both sixty-five 
and seventy is going to increase very considerably relative to the number of persons between twenty and sixty-four-the years in which people are supposed to work-and more so relative to the wage earners and therefore income tax payers in that last group. The proposal in the bill under discussion is expected to cost the dominion and provinces some $92 million in 1948 without allowing for provincial supplements. By 1961 that scheme as it stands would cost $134 million.
The proposals as put forward in the dominion-provincial discussions in 1945, providing for $30 a month with no means test at seventy and with a means test from sixty-five to sixty-nine, would cost an estimated $299 million for the age seventy group and an additional $40 million for the sixty-five to sixty-nine group. This is, of course, an estimate and based on certain assumptions. If the same proportions were to come in from sixty-five to sixty-nine as are expected to come in under the means test from the seventy and over group, this $40 million would be increased to $62 million.
Various other schemes could be considered with and without a means test. The cost without the means test is a simple one to estimate if one relies on the population forecasts of the dominion bureau of statistics, but with a means test the cost of even the present proposal is nothing more than a good guess. The higher the allowable income is raised the harder it is to arrive at any reasonable figure because of the lack of information upon income of persons sixty-five years and over. In the 1941 census for example, we do know that some
30.000	persons between sixty-five and sixty-nine were gainfully employed with incomes above $500, wdiile some 22,000 were gainfully employed with incomes less than $500. The corresponding figures for persons seventy years and over were some 12,000 with incomes over $500, and 9,000 with incomes under $500. These were within a total population of 306,000 in the sixty-five to sixty-nine age group, and
459.000	in the age seventy group, thus leaving a very large number of unknown incomes from investment and other sources where the persons were not such as to be designated as gainfully employed.
If the Ontario figure of $40 a month were to be adopted, say with no means test at seventy and a means test between sixty-five and sixty-nine, the cost would run from around $326 million in 1948 to around $464 million in 1961.
The most popular suggestion among opponents of the present proposals is that of $50 a month, presumably with no means test and everybody over sixty-five to be eligible. This

Old Age Pensions
would cost some S560 million in 1948 and $769 million in 1961. It might be remarked at this stage that the estimated revenue from personal income tax in. the fiscal year 1947-1948 will be $515 million, and in the following year, when the present income tax changes are fully effective, this sum will be even less. Thus the cost of this proposal would very shortly exceed the total revenue from personal income tax by $100 million, with the difference becoming even greater as the number of older people increases and the rates of income tax at least remaining about the same.
Suppose a means test were provided with the $50 a month at sixty-five and the maximum income were limited to $600 inclusive of pension, this might well cut the cost of the preceding figures in half; and it would also provide $50 for everyone at sixty-five, but it certainly would cut most of the incentive for thrift from people who, in their working lifetime, could save with a view to having a retiring income in the neighbourhood of $600, or slightly more.
The drastic suggestion of the Social Credit party, calling for old age pensions at sixty and no means test, would cost $508 million if the pension were $30 a month, and some $847 million if the pension were $50. By 1961 the $50 pension would cost $1,105 million. Looking now at the relative increase in the population forecasts we see that the number of persons over sixty-five to every thousand persons aged twenty to sixty-four will be increasing from 132 in 1948 to 159 in 1961. That is, no matter which of the various schemes is decided upon, the cost of it is going to fall on a relatively smaller number of persons, assuming that the greater part of the greater source of revenue is going to come from the twenty to sixty-four age group. If we consider the number of gainfully employed,
we find that from 234 persons over sixty-five who might be eligible for old age pensions in 1948, there will be 281 of the same class to every thousand of the gainfully employed persons from twenty to sixty-four who will be providing a good part of the money necessary for old age pensions.
The number of income tax payers who would be apt to blame the old age pensions for the highness of their income tax is hard to estimate, since in 1945 there were about 2,180,235, while in 1941 there were only 871,488. If one were to take 1941 as perhaps a standard figure, and were to give pensions to everyone sixty-five years and over, then there would be more persons receiving pensions than there would be paying income tax.
It would take a little while to read this table, and I would ask the permission of the house to put it on Hansard. 'It is a table of costs for nine different plans, all of which have been proposed here. It includes a forecast of the number of people over seventy in the period 1948 to 1961, and also those between sixty-five and sixty-nine, and the total of the two.
There may be some questions about the number of 556,000 over seventy in 1948. It will be found that because of certain tables in the Canada Year Book for 1947 the figures as of that date are not the 1948 figures but rather, as I understand, the 1941 figures. In 1941 there were 459,000 elderly people over seventy, so that what is given here is, I believe, accurate. With the permission of the house I will put these statements on Hansard.

speechtext:
I
should like to start by complimenting the hon. member for Victoria, B.C. (Mr. Mayhew) on the speech he has made, because I realize what an exceedingly difficult speech it must have been for him to deliver. Coming as he does from the southern portion of Vancouver island, I know well that there is not an individual in the whole of British Columbia whose heart is warmer and who personally adopts a more generous attitude than the hon. gentleman. However, on this occasion he has to play the role of Mr. Hyde to the minister's Dr. Jekyll, because he is parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance and therefore may not feel at liberty to speak from his heart but must speak from the figures he has obtained from the study of his statistics.
I have not had the opportunity of studying those statistics. If I speak today I shall perhaps speak somewhat more from my heart than from my head. I also come from the southern end of Vancouver island, and I also claim a high percentage of elderly people living in my constituency, people who have borne the brunt of the great days of our expansion, people who went out many years ago to the prairies and struggled in those homestead days. As a homesteader myself I know something of the hardships of homesteading, although I cannot appreciate the hardships undergone by the earlier settlers, those who today are in the sixty-five to seventy class.
Those people from the prairies moved out to British Columbia partly because the climate is milder, partly perhaps because of the scenery, partly because they thought that the dollars they had saved would carry them further in the milder climate of British Columbia, and perhaps because in more recent years they have realized that the old age pension paid in British Columbia is higher than that paid in some other provinces.
We have therefore a large number of these elderly people who have come to the southern portion of Vancouver island. Many of these come from the prairies. Many of these in the days when labour was cheap, interest was high and the cost of living was low, thought they had saved enough money to take care of

their old age. Now the days of low wages have gone. We have high wages today. The days of high interest rates have also gone, and investments made twenty or thirty years ago by the savings of people who have tried to exercise the quality of thrift do not bring to them anything like the returns that they had hoped would be brought in in their more advanced years.
I am quite certain that the strain of toil and the hardships they experienced in their earlier years when they were building up our western country are taking their toll in the health of these people in their more advanced years, with the result that, with diminishing income from the savings which they have put into bonds, they find they have not enough today to meet the higher cost of living. Their capital is diminishing because they have had to pay hospital expenses, which in the pride of their youth and middle age they never thought they would have to incur. The result is that many elderly people living in my constituency are scraping along in the greatest possible difficulty.
I have visited their shacks, not in the main part of Victoria but in the outlying districts, and there is poverty there among elderly people. It has been said that the younger people of today, the sons and daughters, should provide for their parents in their advanced years. I know that is the philosophy that was accepted perhaps forty years ago when it was regarded as the responsibility of the son or daughter to keep the father and mother in their declining years. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that is the philosophy that might be interpreted in the words of the catechism, where one is exhorted to be content to live in that state of life to which it has pleased Almighty God to call him. But I suggest to you also that the majority of hon. members would not be sitting here in this house if they had been content to accept that philosophy. It was because they were not prepared to accept the circumstances of life into which it had pleased God to call them in their early days that they or their fathers migrated to this country to help to build up their substance and livelihood here.

Old Age Pensions
I think it is a mistake-it is an attempt to continue the trend of an age which has gone by-to suggest that the sons and daughters of the poor are responsible for keeping their parents in their old age, because the sons and daughters of the poor have had additional handicaps to overcome in order to get their education. Surely we are not going to ask the sons and daughters of our poorer inhabitants to carry the responsibility of providing for their parents in their old age. I suggest we have come to a more enlightened era, and that the people as a whole are prepared to look after the aged of this land.
I am not going to repeat all the arguments which have been advanced, I think from all sides of the house, pointing out that the provisions made in this bill are not adequate. I am sure I am speaking for a great many people from the southern portion of Vancouver island when I say it will be with bitter disappointment that they learn of the extent to which the government is prepared to help them at the present day by the increases in the old age pension and by the slight relaxation of some of the regulations in connection with what one may call the means test. There will be bitter disappointment because those aged people had been buoyed up with the hope that a more generous contribution was to be made to them. The feeling amongst a great many of the working men on Vancouver island is such that they would welcome an opportunity of being able to provide for their future by some form of compulsory savings. I dislike the term "compulsion", but we have to remember the outlook of the younger men- In my day we drove teams for a living, and we spent our money freely. While the logger's of today spend their money freely too, many of them have told me that the bugbear before them is the fear of a poverty-stricken old age, and that they would welcome a scheme which would force them to contribute towards some provision for that period in their lifetime. We cannot wait longer.
It is with regret that I see this rather halfhearted measure which has been brought in. I intend, however, to support the bill, because I wTould not deny for another day the meagre increase which is being granted to the aged people. I hope the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) is really serious when he says that this is only intended to be a first step forward, however short that step may be.
There is just one other point I should like to refer to, and it has to do with the blind. Reference was made last night by the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret) to the desirability of granting pension to the blind 83166-296
at an earlier age. In the interests both of the blind themselves and of the national economy, I should like to urge that the pension be paid to our Canadian blind at an earlier age than forty. It may be desirable to pay it at sixteen, or at twenty-one. During those years between twenty and forty the blind man is learning a trade. If he can be given assistance to enable him to go on and learn a trade, it seems to me that he will have a reasonable opportunity of making a livelihood later on in life. But if on the other hand he is denied an opportunity-because he is not granted that pension until he reaches the age of forty- of taking the courses which are necessary in order that he may learn that trade, it seems to me that he will never learn the trade but will always be a burden on the state. I am not at all certain that the whole matter of pensions to the blind should not be removed entirely from the Old Age Pensions Act. They are two entirely separate forms of pension; the conditions which are applicable to the aged are not applicable to the blind.
I hope that at some future time the Minister of National Health and Welfare will give careful consideration to the possibility of bringing in a separate act for pensions for the blind. But in the meantime I hope he will give consideration to reducing, from forty to twenty-one, or even to sixteen, the age limit at which the blind may first receive their pensions. I know that is the desire of many of the societies which look after the blind, because I have had letters from British Columbia urging that such a step be proposed.

speechtext:
I had
not intended to take part in this debate, Mr. Speaker, but in view of some of the statements which were made by some hon. members on the opposite side of the house, I feel obliged to make a few comments at this time. The people of Canada have waited for a considerable length of time for this bill amending the Old Age Pensions Act. High promises were made during the war. At no time were those promises greater than they were during the war loan campaigns which were conducted in this country. As a result of those promises, the hopes and expectations of the people were raised to a high level. Today the people remember that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) said then that unless that new order were well on its way before the end of the war, the people might look for it in vain. The people are now beginning to wonder whether they are to look in vain for that new order. They are wondering whether or not those fine promises made by the federal government during the war were just bribes

Old Age Pensions

for the purpose of getting them to make the sacrifices which were essential in order that we might win the war. I would say that the legislation now before the house is an insult to our senior citizens and, to my mind, constitutes a deliberate breach of faith on the part of the government. I realize that the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) has told us that this is merely a breathing spell. But surely, two years after the war, the old age pensioners have a right to expect to do more than just breathe. They have a right to expect to eat, to live and to clothe themselves in comfort. No one, by the wildest stretch of imagination, could say that this bill will provide a decent standard of living for our senior citizens.
I do not intend to go into any detailed criticism of the bill. However, in passing I should just like to say, as other members of this group have said, that I criticize the bill for the following reasons. It does not increase the pension to $50 a month; it does not provide for reducing the age to sixty; it does not eliminate the means test; and it does not provide for paying a full pension to a married couple where only the husband is of pensionable age. I realize that it provides for the couple being able to have an increased amount of income of their own, but at the present time it does not provide for paying any pension to the wife if she is under pensionable age. We believe the act could very well be modelled along the lines of the War Veterans' Allowance Act, which provides a full pension to married people, no matter what the age of the wife may be.
Furthermore I cannot see any reason why a blind person must reach the age of forty before receiving a pension. Surely a blind person at the age of thirty may be in just as great need of help as one at the age of forty. We feel that the age in respect of blind persons should have been reduced to twenty-one. I have never heard any justification for the level being set at forty.
Furthermore we believe a pension should be paid to all people who are physically incapacitated and therefore unable to take care of themselves. The minister has made it clear that he believes in a contributory scheme. As a matter of fact I believe the majority of the parties in the house, apart from this group, have taken a similar line. But I suggest that those who argue along that line fail to remember, as was pointed out by the leader of this group, that the scheme we now have is a contributory one. I say that because in order to receive the benefits under the act the individual must have been contributing to the general consolidated revenue fund of this country for the past twenty years, either
[Mr. Quelch.l
through direct or indirect taxation, or both. And let us not forget that today around a billion dollars is taken from the people in indirect taxation. It is becoming the greatest source of revenue. Therefore all those people who have been in the country for twenty years have been contributing daily-

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
No matter how poor they are.
Mr. Q.UELCH: -to the fund from which pensions are paid. Therefore what possible argument can there be that we should have some form of contributory scheme, when in fact we already have one?
So long as production is limited, it means that everyone has to be willing to have just a little bit less in order that persons of pensionable age may obtain a pension. On the other hand, if we can develop the resources of this country to their fullest extent, and maintain the national income at around $12 billion, which should be possible, then it would be possible to pay substantial pensions to these persons without reducing the standard of living of the rest of the people.
To those who believe in another type of contributory scheme, let me say this: There is nothing to prevent an individual from indulging in that type of contributory scheme today, if he so desires. He may do so by taking out a government annuity. But the individual with whom I am concerned is the one who is not financially able to do that. No form of contributory scheme will help that individual; and there are many thousands of them.
The minister has argued that there is nothing tp prevent the provinces from increasing the amount of pension, if they so desire. Time and again members have asked, "What is your province going to do?" I would remind the minister of what was said yesterday by the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Hlynka), that this was not the stand taken by the Prime Minister in June, 1931. But I would argue this phase of the question from a different point of view, because people's ideas change, and perhaps the ideas held today by the Prime Minister are quite different froih what they were in 1931. I can well believe that any man who went through the thirties in office would change his opinion.
The obvious reason why the responsibility must rest with the federal government is that that government alone has the power to control the issue of currency and credit, and to control it in terms of public need. That is the familiar phrase used to a great extent by the Prime Minister during the campaign of 1935. It is possible that since then he has changed his mind with regard to whose responsibility

Old Age Pensions
it is to pay old age pensions. He probably realized that the only governing body in Canada which would have the power or the ability to pay a substantial old age pension is that body with the power to control the issue of currency and credit, because he then warned the people of the great danger we faced from certain money barons, and promised that he would institute measures effectively to control them. In fact he went so far as to say that a great battle would ensue in parliament.
What is the situation when a government fails to maintain the proper control of currency and. credit, so that it is available in terms of public need? We saw what happened in the thirties. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance told us about the way in which the pioneers worked, and that they obtained little for their work. He seemed to be under the impression that people should be prepared to do the same today, and that the ones who are working are able to obtain a far greater amount for their work than they were in those days. But let us remember that the same people went through the thirties. Many of them had saved. What happened to the savings of those people in the thirties? Did what happened in the thirties encourage people to save for the future? Many people in the thirties had their total life savings wiped out. Some of them had been contributing to life insurance policies for years, and lost these policies. Life insurance policies were being cancelled on a wholesale scale. What guarantee is there that exactly the same situation will not occur in the future? And if that situation develops again, of what help will a contributory scheme be? It will be just a similar sacrifice.
Many hon. members on the other side of the house have asked: Where will the money come from to pay pensions of the kind you are advocating? I certainly regret to hear that cry echoing through these halls once more, because that was the cry we heard from 1935 to 1939, when we had half a million people unemployed, when we had a great number of people in dire need in Canada; and when time and again members in the house suggested effective measures should be instituted to take care of those people we always heard the same old cry from members on that side of the house: Where will the money come from? Then the minister of finance of that day would tell us, "It is not possible to raise any more money by taxation, and the only money the government of Canada can get is the money it obtains from the pockets of the people." We hear exactly the same cry today.
The hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) tells us he has listened to social credit for three years and does not yet understand it. Let me ask him this: Does he understand the present financial system? I am satisfied he does not. I tell him it is easier to understand social credit than to understand the present financial system, because social credit is based upon reason while the present financial system is not.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Nobody else here understands social credit, either.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
Between 1935 and 1939, when this government was in power, we were told there was no money to provide essential services to the people of this country, that there was no money available to put people to work. And yet, within six weeks of the declaration of war the government found another way. They got the chartered banks to create for their own use $200 million of new money; and speaking in the house the then minister of finance said that the money was created in order to provide employment. If within six weeks of the declaration of war $200 million in new money could be created to provide employment for the people of Canada, why could it not have been done six months before war was declared?
Let hon. members opposite remember that well, for not once in any year during the war did we ever finance the war by taxation, or by borrowing savings alone. Nearly $5 billion in new money was created during that time.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: That is why we have inflation now, is it not?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
No. We have it for the simple reason that fifty per cent of the production was drained away to meet war needs. If that fifty per cent of production had been available to the people, there would have been no inflation, and we would have had the highest standard of living this country has ever known.
But it took a war to force the government to change its financial policy. It is a strange thing that the government are prepared to adopt a sound financial system-and I should not use the word "sound"-to adopt a financial system which will make it possible to maintain production at the highest level during a period of war, in order to save their skins, but they are not prepared to adopt it in peace time to meet the needs of old age pensioners.
During the war we heard time and again the cry that no financial limitation would be allowed to impede the war effort, that the only limit to our war effort would be the men
Old Age Pensions

and materials available to carry it out. Apparently it is no longer a question of men and materials; it is a question of how much we can afford, where we shall get the money, or what will be the financial cost. I should like to say that it is not a question of whether we can afford to do this; but rather, that we cannot afford not to do it. If we want the present system to survive; if we want to retain those things for which we fought, then I say that we shall have to make goods available to people who are aged and physically incapacitated. Otherwise we shall certainly be guilty of hypocrisy in so far as what we said during the war is concerned, and I am now referring to what the government said.
I will give another reason why we cannot afford not to adopt measures of this kind today. I should like to refer to what was said by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) in his budget speech. In that speech the minister intimated that we cannot expect to maintain the present high level of production, the present high level of income and the present level of employment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I do not want to interrupt the hon. gentleman, but I am sure he will agree that he is going a little far afield.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: I believe that what I am now saying has a greater bearing upon whether or not we can afford to pay 150 a month to the old age pensioners than anything that has been said since the debate started. I think the minister will agree that the main reason why pensions are not increased at the present time is the cost. Will the minister deny that? He said that the provinces should do this, but I have pointed out that the provinces cannot hope to be able to do it unless a financial policy is adopted which will maintain prosperity in this country so that they will be able to find the money with which to do it.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: And because of gifts to other countries.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
I think the minister will appreciate that I am coming right to the point. The Minister of Finance said that we could not hope to maintain the high levels of income, employment and production because of a lack of effective demand. That was due, first of all, to the fact that war savings were being spent rapidly and would soon be exhausted; second, that our programme of reconversion was rapidly approaching its end, and, third, that the foreign credits which had been made available to other countries in order that they might buy our goods would soon be exhausted. When that time is reached there will be a lack
of effective demand and no industry can continue to produce unless it can sell its production.
This is the point I wish to make to the minister. One of the finest ways to maintain effective demand in this country is to pay a decent pension to our old age pensioners. I gathered from the statement of the parliamentary assistant that the cost of paying pensions of $50 a month at age sixty-five would be around $508,000,000, and that the cost of paying pensions of $50 a month at age sixty would be around $1,000,000,000. We remember that during the 1930's the United States and Canada adopted minor pumppriming operations. It is now realized by all economists that the reason for the failure of those experiments was that they were not on a large enough scale. The reason for the tremendous increase in production during the war was that large sums of money were spent which, in turn, created a great demand for goods.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons

speechtext:
I believe the hon. member is going beyond the scope of this bill. He has entered into a discussion of our financial system, a discussion which would be more appropriate to a budget debate. I suggest that he endeavour to confine his remarks more directly to the bill which is before the house and which relates to old age pensions.
Mr. QUE'LCH: I doubt if you could tell me how we are to finance old age pensions of $50 a month at age sixty, but I am trying to point out, through you, Mr. Speaker, how that can be done. There is no use in my saying that it can be done without suggesting ways and means whereby' it can be done.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: The hon. member was discussing what took place during the 1930's, and I hardly think that such a discussion would fall within the scope of this bill.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: To come back again to the statement made by the parliamentary assistant that it would cost around a billion dollars to pay pensions of $50 a month at age sixty, we found it quite convenient to provide foreign credits of around $2,000 million extending over a number of years, and during the war we found it quite convenient to make a gift of a billion dollars to Britain in one year. I suggest that, if it were possible to make a gift of one billion dollars to Britain during the war it should be possible to make a gift of a billion dollars to our old age pensioners.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: Every year?

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
That would help to maintain our production at the high level of $12,000

Old Age Pensions
million a year. Do hon. members remember what our income was before the war? I do not want to discuss that because I would be ruled out of order, but our production today is more than double what it was before the war. The result is that we have at least one-half more income today than we had before the war. If anyone had suggested in 1930 that we could double our production and income in three years he would have been laughed at. I do not think anyone will dare to challenge the statement that our income can be maintained at a level of $12,000 million a year. The Minister of Finance told us that the level of production this year will be around $12,000 million, and if we can maintain our income at that level we should have no difficulty in maintaining old age pensions at a satisfactory level even if it cost the country around one billion dollars.
After all, it is not a question of money; it is just a question of goods. It is merely a question of whether or not we in this country can produce a sufficient amount of goods to give our old age pensioners a standard of living of at least $50 a month. That is all it amounts to. Surely we can follow out the same policy which was followed during the war that no financial restrictions shall be allowed to impede our peace effort; that the only limitation will be the men and materials available. If goods are available to provide old age pensioners with an income of $50 a month, then it is up to the government to see that the financial policy of this country is such that that can be made possible.
Before closing, I should like to refer to one statement made by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) during this debate. This is a statement which he has made on several occasions in the house during this session. I presume it is supposed to be a bit of profound wisdom. The minister has said that the only real money is that which is hard to get. Let me say to the minister that that kind of statement does not come well from a Minister of Labour, because a hard money policy is a deflationary policy and, under a deflationary policy, unemployment increases. It seems strange that the Minister of Labour should advocate in this house what in reality is a deflationary policy under which labour would suffer greatly.
