Mr. Speaker, like the previous speaker (Mr. Quelch) I had no intention of taking part in this debate, but I should like to make two suggestions to the government which may be of value in the future. I should like to suggest to the previous speaker that he read this
legislation and study it. I am sure the province of Alberta will be very happy to contribute to their old age pensioners the amount which they may now meet under the statute.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext: If the dominion would keep their hands out of our pockets, probably we could.

subtopic: INCREASES IN AMOUNTS AND INCOME ALLOWANCE REQUIREMENTS-MODIFICATIONS OF ELIGIBILITY
speechtext:
This is a delicate matter and one that should be gone about carefully, honestly and sincerely. It is not one about which statements should be glibly made. When people get around the conference table, as many members of this house hare seen at the dominion-provincial conference, and the Minister of Justice asks one provincial premier how much he wants in dollars and cents for the rental of certain taxation privileges, and the provincial premier gets up, wrings his hands, and eloquently talks about everything else, including the weather, and then sits down, how can you hope to come to an agreement with such people? However, that is not the purpose of my remarks today. I am making no apologies for taking up the time of the house very briefly on this bill, because other duties in the house have made it impossible for me to take the part in its debates that I would like to have taken.
One of the greatest ills that inflict mankind today is fear, the fear of poverty, which coupled with the fear of old age brings on the fear of disease and of pestilence. I would therefore like to commend the government on this step which it has taken. As the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) so eloquently said last night, this is merely one step, but it is a very valuable and worthwhile step, and I commend the government for taking it. I think we are all agreed that it is one of the steps towards the goal towards which we are heading. I know that the government is conscious of that fact.
Persons of advanced age are not desirous of getting something for nothing. I know that the government is conscious of that fact and that it is trying to work out a system of contributory old age pensions which will be paid as of right' to all needy individuals who have attained a stated age. I do not suggest of course that such a plan would eliminate all disease, but it would go a considerable way in bringing comfort and contentment for people of advanced years. It would eliminate many of the mental ills with which they are confronted, and would thereby prolong human existence.
One suggestion I would like to make-and this was ably covered by the hon. member for Halton last evening-is with regard to persons suffering from total disability caused by diseases such as arthritis and paralysis. I am
Old Age Pensions

sure all members of the house are pleased that the government has included in the bill provision for persons who have become incapacitated by blindness. I recall no one in the house saying that he was not in favour of it. The door has thus been opened. There is a large class of people who are afflicted with other diseases which partly or wholly incapacitate them, and these people are in a position similar to if not worse than that of those I have mentioned. Members of the house will recall many cases in their own experience. I remember one of my constituents, an unmarried woman of advancing years, who has done a great deal of good in her community both in public and private matters. I know that such persons, who have no income whatsoever, would be greatly benefited by a provision of the kind which is being made for the blind.
Some time ago I had some correspondence with a friend who is suffering from a form of paralysis which unfits him from earning a living. This gentleman forwarded to me a copy of a resolution which has been submitted to members of the house. I do not know that it went any farther. It was from the Council for Guidance of the Handicapped of Vancouver, British Columbia. While the resolution did not specifically ask for a pension for the handicapped, I am sure it would be of great advantage to them. Since the door has now been opened I think the government would be well advised to take under advisement in due time assistance to people who are suffering from such handicaps as these.
There is another class of persons who have not so far as I am aware been mentioned in this debate. There are over 130,000 persons over whom the Dominion of Canada has legislative control which amounts to a form of wardship. I refer of course to the Canadian Indians, the first residents of this dominion. A great many of them have not had the opportunities and the background of education which members of this house have had, but I am sure that if they were given an opportunity to help themselves, free from unrfeasonable restrictions and free to enjoy a sense of equality, they would do great credit to this country. Here again, however, the fear of poverty and old age has given many of them a sense of inferiority and frustration which finds expression in resentment and unrest. I know that the government is giving consideration to these matters. The house recently adopted a report of the Indian affairs committee recommending the giving of old age pensions to the Indians. While realizing that the provinces make some contribution to old age pensions, I would urge upon the federal government, whose wards

these Indians are, that some form of pension be introduced at an early date for the benefit of our Indian population. I am sure that the expenditure involved would be of great assistance in raising the standards of our Indian population and in carrying out the endeavour of the Indian affairs committee, to help the Indian help himself.

Mr. Speaker, I attempted to get into this debate immediately after the speech of the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge), so that I might congratulate him upon his delightful language and upon his ability to tell stories of the pioneering days in British Columbia. I wish he could be persuaded to write a book of those experiences so that they may have a wider circulation.
We are all anxious that this bill should reach the committee stage, and I shall delay the house for only a moment or two so that I may put on the record, in what I hope will be a concise and brief form, those things in which this bill is to the members of this group something of a disappointment. In the first place, I think the bill provides too little money for people of pensionable age. Second I think the pensionable age is too high. Third I think that the bill provides, even with the increase to S30, a standard of living no better than $20 was before the period of the war.
Next I would say that the bill does not abolish the means test. I would say that it puts the responsibility for the payment of the increased pension upon the provinces, and by so doing, at a time when national unity is the thing which this country needs above all others, it continues the dominion-provincial dog fight and initiates an interprovincial one. Next it does not provide that old age pensions should be, as I think they should be, a purely dominion responsibility. It does not provide that uniformity of pension which we think is desirable across the country,
When one examines the bill closely he finds that it does not imply that any province of necessity must increase its pension; it merely guarantees 'to that province seventy-five per cent of whatever amount the province decides to pay, up to $30. But if that province, as I interpret the bill, decides to pay a lesser amount, there is no reason, so far as this bill is concerned, why the province should not do so.
In view of the small amount of increased payment under this bill, we must take notice that it does not provide for any medical services or any supplemental benefits for persons over seventy such as is provided, for instance, in Saskatchewan and in some other

Old Age Pensions
provinces. While I am speaking of the western provinces, I might say that I do not think this bill really provides an increase in pensions in the four western provinces at all, unless those four provinces decide to carry on these supplemental benefits which they have been paying and which, I am quite sure, were considered as a temporary amelioration pending the agreement between the provinces and the dominion, or pending legislation by which the dominion would assume its proper responsibilities.
Finally, I think we should consider that the sections of the bill which is now before the house are a sufficient proof that what Canada needs is an over-all measure of social security for all the people of Canada upon a dominion basis.

One could talk at great length on this important social measure, but I shall be brief. I feel that I should like to make a contribution to the debate and draw to the attention of the minister and the government what I consider the true position today. The real challenge is for the government to institute the proposals they made to the provinces in 1945. They still have access to the same fields of taxation that they had at that time. It would have been accepted as evidence of good faith had they written into the Old Age Pensions Act $30 a month without a means test. I could talk at considerable length with respect to the means test. I consider that the means test puts a premium upon thrift. In other words, as one grows older he approaches old age with the fear that his resources are insufficient. Realizing that he must reduce his resources still further in order to claim a pension, he is more apt to do so.
The provinces have sought, within the limit of their resources to deal generously with the pensioners. Ontario is particularly to be complimented on instituting almost immediately an over-all .pension, depending upon the passage of this legislation, of $40 a month, subject, of course, to need. In addition to that, Ontario provides many other social benefits, which were referred to by the previous speaker, to the old people. If we had the pension that was promised of $30 a month without the means test the people would then feel a sense of security, and that thej' were being rewarded for services rendered. Of course, when I speak of the removal of the means test I do not mean that it should be compulsory to accept old age pensions as we understand family allowances today. That is to say, I am suggesting that it should be necessary only to prove your age if you
want to receive a pension, and that the pension likewise would be subject to taxation. If your income were sufficient without the pension and you obtained the pension only to increase it within taxable limits some of it would be returned.
Another matter, which was touched upon by the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) and which I wish to underline and bring to the attention of the minister and of the government is the position in which we find the old people in the Indian tribes today. It has been my privilege to serve on the Indian affairs committee. Recently we passed a resolution urging upon the government that they give consideration to granting old age pensions to Indians. After that resolution was passed, numerous delegations who appeared before the Indian affairs committee dwelt upon the fact that this was one of the finest things the committee had done. The chairman, fortunately, cautioned them to understand that it had not yet been enacted but was only a recommendation on our part.
The very fact that the bill removes the nationality clause from the requirements seems to me to provide a challenge to the government to give consideration to the Indians. Because of their standard of living, I am sure that they would be satisfied with even a lesser pension than has been provided for the average Canadian citizen. The old Indians on reserves are living in deplorable conditions. They receive just a small pittance. From my experience the top limit is about $5.60 a month, and that must provide them with fuel, clothing and food. Hon. members can understand that even $15 or $20 a month to an Indian would be very acceptable. Therefore, on their behalf I make this special plea, that consideration be given to our first citizens now that we have taken the nationality requirements out of the act. Surely those who were the first citizens of this land, those whom we are seeking to absorb into our society and to build up, should be entitled to consideration.
I have said before, and I repeat that there should be a change in the title of the act. The act should read the "Retirement Pensions Act." We should emphasize constantly the objective, which is to bring about retirement so that the labour field may be left to those who are still able to earn, instead of emphasizing old age pensions.
During my municipal life I served on the old home board in Grey county. Some years ago we changed the name of that institution to the Grey county home. I know there are still places where such institutions are described as poorhouses, houses of refuge or old people's homes, and so on. I think these
Old Age Pensions

things mean a great deal to the old people. In Grey county we have done away with such names as the old people's home, or the house of refuge, and so on. With respect, I say that the old age pension should be considered a retirement pension available at the age set forth in the bill. If that were done it would be greatly appreciated.
I say further, and with this I conclude, that the government could afford to deal more liberally with the blind and with those who are totally incapacitated physically, who are a great charge upon their families and are likely to become a charge upon society. In the initial stage I do not think the pension should be the full amount that would finally be awarded to an elderly person; but it should be an award, a subsistence allowance, and yet still cause the individual to exercise his own initiative and to develop his ability to earn a living for himself. I do not believe that any pension should be of such a size as either to encourage indolence or to discourage ambition and enterprise. Rather is it a reward for services, and therefore we should seek to remove from it anything that would leave the recipients feeling that they are objects of charity.

Mr. Speaker, it is agreed, at least on this side, that the present bill is a sorry answer to the plea of the Canadian people for more humane and effective treatment of their aged. The offer to pay three-quarters of an additional $5 to those provinces which agree to pay up to $30 a month, that is to say, $3.75 per pensioner per month, is clearly not enough to take care even of the increased cost of living and, therefore, it means little.
My main objection is to the means test. The application of that test has a demoralizing effect on the old age pensioner. I have laid a great deal of experience with the aged in my community. I live in a constituency where many old people are unable to qualify for the pension 'because previously they did not have the language qualification that was called for, and now the courts decide that they have not sufficient knowledge of the operations of our democratic way of life. I think the Canadian people would support the abolition of the means test, and I know something of the vicious effect it has on the health of the people.
A few dollars put by for their old age is extremely valuable to them, but the effect of the	means test is to lower their
own self respect because they feel that they are paupers having to accept charity from society. I wish every member could have

seen the change that took place in the old age pensioners in our province when that government instituted free hospitalization, free medical care, free drugs, free dental and free eye treatment for old age pensioners. Let me refer to one man of seventy-five who had been gradually going blind. He had no money to pay doctor's fees to have his eyes cared for and he had become totally blind. A couple of years ago he received a card notifying him that as an old age pensioner he could get free medical treatment. He went to the doctor, who looked at his eyes and decided that an operation would cure that man, and the result is that today he can see. Twenty five dollars is very little for a person over seventy years of age to live on, and when such a person has to go and confess to a doctor that he has no money to pay him he is placed in a mean position and would rather not go. The relief which would be given by the government in taking over the obligation of seeing that these people shall have the medical and dental treatment and drugs which they need but cannot provide for themselves would be a greater step forward than anything I know.
Apparently the government in this bill indicates that it cannot go farther and cannot give $50. It cannot reduce the age limit. It is making some change in regard to the amount which old persons are allowed to have as income, but few people after seventy can earn much income, and if the government cannot carry out the other reforms that have been suggested I would urge that at least they take some steps to provide medical attention, which means so much to people over the age of seventy.

Having listened to what has been said by hon. members, I find once more that my hon. colleagues have feelings that honour them, concerning .the old people. The old age pension was instituted about twenty years ago, and since then it has been in operation in different provinces. But before 1926-27 there were old people. There were people were living to just as old an age as people live now and they were looked after by their relatives. As I mentioned yesterday, very few had to take action against their children to obtain the support that was due them, and a discussion like the one which has taken place on old age pensions would have been termed uncalled for and untimely and would have surprised the House of Commons.

Old Age Pensions
But in 1925-26 a definite promise was made by the Liberal party in the famous letter to A. A. Heaps, who is now a civil servant and who was then member for Winnipeg South, that there would be an old age pension scheme after the election of 1926-1925 or 1926-and we had it. Now everybody is considered to have the same need. The reasoning is the same as that of the judge who said that all those who practised petty smuggling should be hanged the same as murderers, and the other judge who said he believed in equal justice to all and that the murderers should be fined like those who indulged in petty smuggling; the same justice for all, the same way of reasoning with regard to all the old people.
I know that what my hon. friend who has just spoken has said is true in this sense, that hospitals have done marvels for the old people; but they did marvels for the old people before the institution of the old age pension. How is it that now the state has to look after these people? It is because private charity cannot afford to look after them. But that was done before taxes were so high. When the taxes were not so heavy it was easy for people with means to give part of their income for the building and maintenance of splendid charitable institutions such as we have in the province of Quebec, but with the increase in taxation they cannot do that now and the state has come, in a socialistic manner, to provide similar help for the old and needy.
It is the great difference between two periods. In the first period, we had private enterprise when those who had more money than was necessary for their personal needs decided to give a large share to the public to help young people to get their education, to help the sick and the aged. Now taxes are so high that it is impossible for anyone to do what was done before, and that is why we have this kind of legislation.
I do not know whether I was correctly interpreted-I was not quite correctly interpreted in the press-when I said yesterday that it was possible to provide better health without spending more money. It is absolutely necessary to decide to do something, but not to pay any pension to those who are not in need of it. This will require courage; it will require determination. I understand that while a by-election in Halifax is going on, it is a bad time to make a decision of that kind. The debate on the old age pension is just an auction to bribe the old people of seventy who are not entitled to a pension in the county of Halifax or anywhere else. It
is a bribe; it is an auction. It is said that we must do this and must do that. There is one thing we must do. We must help those who are in need and who have no other support. Among them are children who have no hands. There are others who suffer from infirmities, from young people to the very old. Is it not absurd to decide that it is only at forty that a man who is blind shall have a pension? If a blind man deserves a pension at forty, he deserves it as soon as he is born. We go on like that. A limit is set at forty. The minister will probably say, "I have been so advised by the officials of my department". When will the ministers stop singing that song? When will they make their own decisions? There are some decisions they have to make with their colleagues. How is it that a bureaucrat advises the minister about this policy? It is the policy of his department. Policies of his department should be submitted by him to the council; then the council will decide, and he will stand by that decision in his seat in the house. He should not ask clerks to give him advice on policy. The clerks in his department are there to execute policies. We are here to make them do so by passing laws according to the needs of the Canadian people. I may be wrong, but that is my position. I am humiliated when any minister says, "I will seek the advice of my officials". We see the minister, a man of intelligence, a man of apparent competence, but a man who cannot walk alone without the crutches of his department.
This is a serious matter. I live among certain people who have been kind to me and whom I want to help. Amongst those who receive pensions I know there are some who do not deserve them, but there are some who deserve them fully. Some who do not deserve them, have them just the same; others who deserve them, who should have had them for a long time have positively nothing. This bill will give them nothing. It is made contributory. What is that contribution? It is rad tape, because we already have government annuities. Why have two contributory systems, one in the Department of National Health and Welfare and the other in the Department of Labour, or the Department of Finance. They exchange departments at some point, and I do not know just where it is. However, there is another contributory system already in existence, and I do not see the necessity of putting a tenth wheel on the coach. Contributory! It is nonsense to suggest contributory old age pensions, because those who need them are unable to pay the contribution. That is just as clear as spring water, just as clear as daylight at noon.
Old Age Pensions

I appreciate the fact that the minister invited me to some parleys to discuss the matter of old age pensions. I thank him very much, but I have not been there because I know that any suggestion made by any member is worth nothing unless it is supported by some minor official of the minister's department. So here we are. I will not say any more because it is useless. Some of my colleagues have suggested that I should bring in an amendment to provide for a differentiation, a sorting of those who really need old age pensions and those who do not. I will make no amendment. I have offered some ideas and some suggestions. But I know very well that any suggestion or any amendment made by any member will be useless. Only the bureaucrats run the business. I am sorry, but I have seen people suffering so greatly, people in need, people who are old, that I think it is time their grievances were laid before parliament. I have letters in my pocket to illustrate what I am saying. There are just a few. I have countless letters of the kind. Here is one from a parish priest which says, "I have in parish Mr. and Mrs. So-and-so who are in need. Both are sick. To keep house the wife should have a maid. She is sick	and	he is	deaf.	He also is	sick.He suffers	from	the heart.	In spite of the
allowances and assistance to needy mothers there will be some cases here and there which will not benefit from it."
That is signed by a parish priest. They do not always want to go to the hospital. They could go there under the public assistance regulations, but they want to stay together in their home. With a little help they could	be looked	after,	they could	paythe doctor	and	have	some	assistance.	But
they are given nothing. They have not reached the age of seventy! It is only at seventy that one becomes old and needy! I have numerous letters like that about people who really deserve consideration, people who were well off at one time but who have lost all they had, and others who have been sick- people who deserve consideration. But the limit has been set at seventy, and it will be seventy. The minister is asking $20,000,000 for the needy children of Europe, and I agree to that. We cannot have $1,000,000 to fix up these cases, but we can have $20,000,000 for other children. It is all right to give $20,000,000 to the needy children of Europe, provided that the needy children are not people with long beards. But if it is done for outside, it must be done at home here. Yesterday everybody applauded when it was done for another country. But when we want some help for the people of this

country we cannot have it. Seventy years! It did not happen a long time ago. It happened yesterday. I am in full sympathy with helping everyone who is in need, but why give the same help to those who are not in need? The earth will continue to turn around. People will attach no importance to it. They will say it is all right. Those who suffer far away are of no importance at all. It we make a distinction between those who need the pension and those who do not, we may displease a few. We might just as well let those who are sick and suffering from infirmities continue to suffer. It is all right. We do not see them. They are poor. They are far away. They will not write us. It is just the same as if they did not belong to our own land. That is the way it goes. One could go anywhere, even here in Ottawa, and see people who are suffering. Some people are on the street selling pencils. Is it not a shame for a man to sit on the sidewalk and sell pencils at the door of the big stores in Montreal or even here in Ottawa? That man should have some comfort in life. He has been deprived of his legs, and sometimes of his arms. He is entitled to some comfort Well, they are there on the street; they are all right. It is all right for them. Those men are entitled to pensions as much as some rich men over seventy.
Let me explain how the payment of pensions, and even an increase in the payment, will not cost any more than the amount now spent for old age pensions. Let me point out how it will not cost any more, even if pensions are increased in needy cases. This can be done if the state will get rid of all the parasites who are exploiting the state, who consider the state to be something like a milch cow. They can be put aside, and that money used to increase pensions for the needy so that, if required, they can have their doctors. They can improve their conditions of life and have a few moments of sunshine before quitting this world to go to a better one. The reduction which can be made will be profitable to others; even the government may save money.
I have one further observation, and I shall have finished. In the hearts of the people there is a deep sense of justice. When they see something unjust happening they say there is something wrong. When assistance to the people has certain limitations they wonder why those who are outside are not brought in to be looked after properly. When the right thing is not being done we often hear severe judgment passed by the people, when they say, "We live in an unjust world."

Old Age Pensions
Why is it an unjust world? Because parasites in the Department of National Health and Welfare, whom I have already denounced, are too lazy to do the necessary work of selection. It is impossible to make them move. 1 have already complained about them. They are parasites who come from all over the world. They are not progressive. They are there just for their jobs, and I denounce them as strongly now as I did when the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Mackenzie) had the health branch under his supervision.
The other day I was passing through Montreal. A man shook hands with me and said, "You were right in complaining." He was referring to a one-language official of the department who had been so hard on the bilinguals when he was connected with the air force. I denounced him in the house, and two or three years after he was so grateful he thanked me for what I had done.
I will say they are not all like that. There are a few laudable exceptions. But at the present time it is impossible to bring the attention of the Department of National Health and Welfare to the realities of life. I want them to help those who are poor; I want them to help those who are needy; and if they have to make a sacrifice of the votes of those few who receive pensions without being entitled to them, let us cut the string and give a chance to the needy ones.

I do not wish to take up too much time, and I do not think I will prevent the minister from speaking before six o'clock. In all the years I have been in the house I have always spoken with respect to old age pensions, and I feel
I should like to say something at this time.
I shall be brief, and I have no intention of being technical.
I have listened as usual, to the speeches of hon. members who have preceded me. It seems to me that many of them have occupied themselves with the methods of paying the pension when, as members, we should be concerned only with the policy, and consideration of the question as to whether Canada should pay a better pension to her old people or should be content to continue to pay the pittance the old people are now receiving.
Owing to the increased cost of living, the present pension is not as good as it was before the war, despite the slight increase proposed in the bill. It has been said in the house times without number, and not only by private members but by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King.) himself, that anything physically possible and desirable can be made financially possible. So that what we should concern ouselves with is whether or not we are justified in. increasing the pension to our old people; we should leave methods to experts.
What do the old people need. Merely food, clothing and shelter. So that all we have to ask ourselves is this: Can Canada provide the necessary food, clothing and shelter for the old people? If not, then I suggest that we should have an inquiry into the reason why we cannot, and we should leave off talking about the immense riches of our country.
I do not think any hon. member would doubt for a moment that the productive power of Canada is ample to provide food, clothing and shelter for our old people. Who is to pay for this pension? Obviously, as the then Minister of Finance, the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Ilsley), said during the first days of the war, when the question was asked how the war was to be paid for: "The cost of the war must come out of the current production." And so with old age pensions, the cost must come out of current production. Luckily for our old people, Canada produces more food, clothing and shelter than is needed; we have, a surplus; we are on an exporting basis. Therefore there is no reason why the raising of the standard of living, because that is what it means, of our old people should entail a lowering of the standard of living of the rest of the people. It is true that during a war, when the bulk of the population is engaged in the war effort, either in the armed forces or in making munitions, a reduction in living standards would be reflected by old age pensions. One of the reasons why we in this group did not press the matter too strongly during the war was that we realized that the
Old Age Pensions

war entailed a lowering of the standards of living for everybody. But that time is in the past, and we shall soon be faced with the necessity of finding markets for what we can and do produce. I say with the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) that the needs of our people should come before the needs of any other people in any other country. When our own needs are satisfied, it will be the time to consider the people in other countries.
There is the question of whether these pensions should be contributory or noncontributory. I have always advocated noncontributory pensions, because I can see that a contributory scheme would provide tremendous control over the workers of this country who would be paying into a fund for the greater part of their lives. They could be made to toe the line by a threat of loss of pension rights, and for that reason, among others, I have always opposed a contributory pension scheme.
Some people think that if everyone were thrifty and saved his money there would be no need of old age pensions; they seem to think that those who are not thrifty should be penalized by having to forgo pensions. It seems to me that an old age pension is not given as a reward for thrift; it is paid or should be paid as a right to any human being who arrives at the age or at the state of health which prevents or handicaps him from earning a full living for himself.
What is the opinion of the people of Canada as a whole with regard to this matter? Have they registered their desires in connection with it? From the letters I have received, not only from people in my own riding, but from people all over Canada, there is no doubt in my mind that the vast majority of Canadians favour a larger pension paid at an earlier age. I cannot see why the members of this house should not feel free to reflect the opinions of the majority of the Canadian people. If those people demand a larger old age pension, then it is up to the members of parliament to meet their wishes.
If a vote against this bill did not involve a vote of non-confidence or a vote of censure; if every hon. member voted exactly the way he felt, I have no doubt that there would be an overwhelming vote for larger pensions to be paid at an earlier age. I have let it be known that I intend to vote against the bill.
I have been told by some that people will say I voted against increasing the pension by $5. But, I can imagine the minister who has charge of this bill saying to the cabinet, "I do not believe that the members will agree to such a miserable addition to the pension; 
I think there will be a lot of opposition to it," and I can imagine some other member of the cabinet saying, "They may talk about it but they dare not vote against it; they will be frightened to vote against it because of what their constituents might say."
When I vote against this bill I am not voting against the Liberal government. I am not trying, nor do I hope to defeat the present government. My sole purpose in voting against this bill is to register my protest in the only way I can, to make clear what I think of the miserable pension that is to be paid to our old people. For those reasons and those reasons only I shall be . forced to vote against the bill.

Mr. Speaker, I shall not detain the house for more than five minutes. I have not spoken for some time either on this bill or on the amendment or anything else. I want to point out two things, without, I hope, threshing old straw. In the old age pension aspect of the question I agree largely with the first speech made by the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot). It seems to me that what we are all seeking to do here is to provide help for the needy; and, having listened to this debate, I am convinced that we are not going at that in the proper way. We are piecemealing things rather than having some integrated scheme in Canada to look after our needy people, the needy by age, illness, blindness and in any other way.
It has been stated by some in this house that the dominion government are doing so-and-so and the provinces have the opportunity of making their own additions. That may be true, Mr. Speaker, in two provinces. It is untrue in seven, because seven provinces are on the dole from this dominion government, exactly as it is suggested that the old age pensioner will be on the dole. In other words, those seven provinces have a confined budget, outside of which they cannot expand. That is all I am saying about that.
I wish to say one word with respect to our blind people. I hope the minister when he replies will give some reason why pensions for our blind should not begin until forty years of age. I was very much impressed' by the argument of the hon. member for Outremont (Mr. Rinfret), that a reduction of the pensionable age for the blind from forty to twenty or twenty-one could involve only a very small expenditure. My memory is that it was very small, comparably, in any event. Again I say that when a person has reached that point where he is not a natural charge on his parents as most of us are through our school years-I am not admitting that I

Old Age Pensions
was in that class because I went through school and I earned plenty of money in the holidays in years gone by-I can see no reason and none has so far been advanced by anyone why the pension for the blind should not begin at least when that person becomes of age. I trust that the minister in the kindness of his heart will probably change his mind and agree with that suggestion which seems to meet with general approval from all members of this house. Some hon. members have referred to the government and to my person as indulging in a form of cruelty that should not be countenanced by this house. I think we have just had from the hon. member for Calgary West (Mr. Smith) the kind of approach that one should use in dealing with this problem. No one in this house, no matter where he sits, has in his heart anything but a desire, I am sure, in the light of his responsibilities, to do the right thing for the particular class of people who are covered by this amending bill.

What I suggest to the house is that we realize that what we are debating is a specific and concrete suggestion in the form of a bill. A good bit of the discussion we have heard, some of it emotional-and I am not complaining of that-has had no real relevancy to the actual provisions of the bill as outlined in my initial statement. Some have referred to this measure as a peanut, and so on. Let us see whether that suggestion has any relevancy to the bill.
The financial commitment involved in this bill representing the sum of $20,000,000 is as much as all the provinces combined are now paying in old age pensions. When hon. members say that this bill does not represent a progressive step, when they deny the language of the hon. member for Spadina (Mr. Croll), I do not think they have addressed themselves-and I say this with great respect- to the implications and the clauses of the bill.
Is it out of the question to suggest that another indication of the importance of this measure is the number of new pensioners who will go on pension as a result of this bill? There are 217,000 people of the age of seventy and over who are now receiving old age pensions in Canada. Of those 217,000, some
7,000	are blind persons. There are 539,000 old aged persons in Canada, seventy and over. By this bill, which, on the admission in the opening statement of the government, was said to be not a permanent measure but an interim measure, 60,000 people who have not under the existing law been able to receive one cent by way of old age pension will come under its provisions. To the hon. member for Wetaskiwin (Mr. Jaques), who said that he would vote against this bill, I say that is for him to say, but in voting against this bill he is voting against 60,000 people getting pension for the first time.

I am sure that some hon. members have overlooked the fact-they can dismiss it, but dismissing it does not deal with the issue- that, under this bill, the provisions as to outside income which the pensioner may have and yet get his pension place us ahead of New Zealand, ahead of Australia, ahead of Great Britain.

I sincerely hope so. What I want to point out to the hon. gentleman is

this. In the shadow of his remarks was the implication that if he had the opportunity he would do something that this administration has not had the courage to do. Let us look at the facts of the case. The first proposal for old age pensions by any administration came from the government headed by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) in 1926. That bill was defeated in another place by gentlemen of the same political tinge as my hon. friend. That bill was opposed in this house by the then leader of the Conservative party, the Right Hon. Arthur Meighen, in the most denunciatory terms which I think I have ever read in Hansard, and which are available if my hon. friend wishes to make a similar retort.
Then the hon. gentleman went on to say what he would do and what they would do, free from responsibility, enjoying the luxury of opposition, forgetting that in 1930 there was in this country a Conservative government under the leadership of the present Lord Bennett, at a time when this country was suffering economic deprivations the like of which it had never suffered before. Between 1930 and. 1935 was the time, the special time, when, the old age pensioners had the right, if they ever had the right at any time, to go to a government and ask for relief. But did the government of that day, headed by my hon. friend who is now the leader of the opposition, do anything at that time to improve the status of the old age pensioners? No. At that time my hon. friend was the premier of a province, and let us see what he did when he was the premier of that province.

It was passed on March 17, 1943, and made retroactive to January 1, but it was passed when my hon. friend was no longer a member of the government, but when his ambitions were lying in other channels.
So that the record can be clear, my hon. friend made a speech in this city about eleven weeks ago, speaking at the Chateau Laurier at a banquet of the Progressive Conservative association. I shall now quote from the Ottawa Journal of Saturday, March 29. I should like to place it on record in the light of what my hon. friend said when he replied to my statement, and I ask anj' hon. member to put this statement against w'hat he said they would do, and to judge as to the likelihood of my hon, friend dealing in a responsible way with this matter. He said:
When the cost of paternalism reaches the stage that it lessens production and services, what we then have is not an increase in social security, but a decrease in the material prosperity of all.
Up to now the government has been taxing us five times as high as before the war. Even after it makes its promised reduction, the tax load will be four times as high as before the war. On the basis of its own figures, the government ought to bring in a reduction of 33 per cent all round. Before the war, taxation and other revenues amounted to some $500 million. Owing to the government's extravagance and heavy commitments, it will probably exact $2 billion from the Canadian taxpayer this year.
You cannot ask for a reduction of taxation in one breath and make proposals that will involve commitments in another. It is all very well for an hon. member who has not the responsibility of the leader of the opposition to do that, but the proposals that he made would call upon the administration of this country to expend not less than $340 million. I take second place to no man in this house in my desire to do something for those who can benefit from social security, and my whole life shows it; but I am not going to make political promises when I know full well that these promises, in the light of all other contingent obligations, cannot be realized at the present time.
I could go on and show that it was the same hon. gentleman who expressed certain views about family allowances, but more of that on another occasion. What my hon. friend can do is seriously to consider what I said about the government's over-all security proposals made to the provinces in August,
1945. If he does not accept my assurances I call to witness tke words of the present Minister of Justice (Mr. Usley) when he was Minister of Finance last July, when he said that once we had a fiscal understanding with the provinces, the. government's social security programme represented an essential part of the government's objectives.
I call to witness the statement of the present Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) twice this year, once in Toronto and once in this house.
I call attention to my own statements as a responsible minister of the crown. But if that does not satisfy the hon. gentleman, let me remind him of the words of the Prime Minister in a telegram sent to the premier of Saskatchewan on July 15, 1946, and reiterated three times since in subsequent communications. This is what the Prime Minister of Canada said:
As emphasized in the budget address, the public investment and social security proposals submitted last August remain an essential part of the dominion government's programme. As soon as there is sufficient acceptance of the proposed tax agreements we shall be ready to explore, in a general conference, or otherwise, the possibilities of working out mutually satisfactory arrangements in regard to the whole or any part of our earlier public investment and social security proposals.

I will go farther. The attitude I am taking in this debate today is the attitude which my hon. friend took, speaking on this very floor, in this very building, at the opening of the Rowell-Sirois conference. Let me repeat our view with regard to this matter. On the social security side, the proposals prepare the way for a system of national old age pensions payable at seventy years, with no means test and entirely financed by the federal government. A further programme was proposed of old age assistance at sixty-five to sixty-nine, financed jointly by the provinces and the dominion. That is a responsible undertaking. It is a colossal undertaking
Old Age Pensions

if hon. gentlemen will realize the cost involved-that together with health insurance. I want to see these things done, but I do not want to see the people told that they can be done unless we have the necessary arrangement with those other agencies of government without which we cannot do these things. The hon. member for Vancouver North (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) made a suggestion as to what they thought should be done. Of course, the proposed resolution of theirs would be out of order, but I want them to know that the objectives they have in mind are objectives that this government is anxious, in the light of its commitments, in the light of its arrangements with the provinces, to try to bring about.
Let it not be forgotten that this measure, unimportant as some hon. gentlemen have said it was, will, when it becomes law, represent on the part of this government, and on the part of the provinces, an expenditure of $100,000,000 on old age pensions. I want to see more than old age pensions-the sort of thing the hon. member for Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot) talked about, the sort of thing my colleague the hon. member for Essex West (Mr. Brown) talked about, the sort of thing the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) talked about. Those are things I should like to see done, but those are measures which we shall never bring about if we put every egg we have in one basket. That surely is clear. Those who, like the hon. gentlemen of the Cooperative Commonwealth. Federation, have been advocating $50 a month- which would cost $560 million in 1948, $611 million in 1951, $769 million in 1961 and $914 million in 1971- when they realize what they have really advocated, must, on reflection, conclude that you cannot have a broad system of social security if you enter into such colossal commitments on any one item, without regard to the entire pattern. And are those commitments much more outlandish than the proposal of $60 a month by hon. gentlemen in the rear, which would cost in the years mentioned, $672 million, $733 million, $923 million and $1,097 million?
I want to see health insurance, and I will do all I can to bring it about, but it will not be brought about by an unbalanced programme that does not bear a relation to the whole scheme one has in mind.
I have been charged with criticism because I was shouldering on the provinces a responsibility which they should not be asked to bear. The house will remember that the day after this bill was introduced the province of

DEPARTMENT OF THE SECRETART OF STATE 366. Departmental administration, $126,198.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before the item carries, I should like to discuss a matter of general interest, and what I shall have to

say is not directed particularly to the department now before the committee. However I feel that this item for departmental administration affords me an opportunity of saying what I have in mind.
In recent years parliamentary sessions have been extending far beyond the traditional spaces of time they occupied in former years. While I shall not take time to consult the records, anyone who looks into them will find that in earlier days sessions of parliament were nearly always completed before the end of the period of spring, and that it was seldom they ran into the time of year which, in recent years, has become our custom.
This fact may have had some bearing on the time at which departmental reports have been compiled. What actually happens is that in departmental reports matters which were of interest more than two years before are discussed. For instance, a matter in a departmental report which appears under the date of April, 1945, is now being dealt with in June, 1947. That is a condition which is common in reports coming before the house at this time.
The last report for the Department of the Secretary of State-and I do not criticize this department particularly, because it is common to all-is for the year ended March 31, 1946, and contains information relative to that department as far back as April, 1945. What I am about to say is not said by way of criticism, but rather in an effort to be constructive. My thought is that if we are to overhaul our method of procedure, we ought also to overhaul our system of presenting departmental reports. If we are to continue to sit into July-and apparently we are, from time to time-I believe some change must be made in this regard. The fact that we do sit into the summer months is a fact for which possibly all in the house must accept a share of responsibility.
On the other hand, I believe that we ought not to be asked to deal with something in a departmental report which might be classed as ancient history. I am wondering whether a report of a department such as this one could not be brought down as a report of the fiscal year ending March 31, 1947, rather than 1946.
Immediately the minister's answer, and that of his officials, will be that it is impossible to get the information in time. I fancy, however, that is a specious explanation, because in times of war and peace we have done much more difficult things than compiling reports and having them in shape for presentation at a session of parliament. My suggestion is that departmental reporting should be brought up to date, so that we may not be asked to

Supply-Secretary of State
deal with matters in a report which, on occasions, have developed more than two years earlier. Those events have become ancient history and do not serve as a useful guide as to the activities of the department in question.
I am discussing the matter in a general way because I believe it is something worthy of investigation, with a view to improvement.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I am interested in what has been said by the hon. member for Peel. This afternoon when I learned that the estimates for the Department of the Secretary of State were to be placed before the committee I went to the distribution branch in this building and asked for a copy of the report of the Department of the Secretary of State. Upon being given the report, I took it to my office and commenced looking into it. Upon looking at the front page, I found that the report I had been given was for the year ended March 31, 1946. I went back to the distribution office and asked Mr. Gray if he could let me have a copy of the report of the Department of the Secretary of State for March 31, 1947. He told me it had not yet come out. In looking through the report for 1946, I noticed a heading, "Naturalization branch", and I suppose in the report for 1947 that heading would be changed to "Citizenship branch". There would be a lot of information under that heading dealing with the period up to March 31, 1947, which is not in the report that was handed to me.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I must say that I have a lot of sympathy with the hon. member for Peel. I have always thought that reports were not presented soon enough for the convenience of members of parliament. subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
What steps are being taken to provide adequate accommodation for the patent office? During the consideration of the bill to amend the Patent Act by the banking and commerce committee, evidence was given which satisfied me, and I think it satisfied all members of the committee, that the patent office required more space if it were to carry on its work in a satisfactory manner. Mr. J.	T. Mitchell, commissioner of patents, stated that there were only 12,000 square feet of space, while he had asked for 70,000 square
feet. It certainly was apparent from the evidence given before the committee that more room is required for this work.
Not only is more space required, but additional staff are also required. If there were a staff of fifty patent examiners and 110 to 120 clerks we would be able to handle these patent applications much more satisfactorily. I realize that there is difficulty in getting more staff and in training these men, and there is the question of adequate salaries and the losses incurred by men leaving their positions and taking positions with private firms. The housing situation is another problem. There may be men, who would like to take positions, but when they look into the housing situation they decide not to go any further with their applications. What steps are being taken to obtain adequate staff?
It may come as a surprise or perhaps even as a shock to hon. members to know that, because of insufficiency of office space and inadequacy of staff in the patent office, the average length of time between the filing of an application for a patent and the date when the examination is commenced is eighteen months. Evidence was given before the committee that in the case of 121 patents which had been issued on February 25 last, a period of three years had elapsed between the filing of the application and the granting of the patent.
Something should be done about enlarging the space in order that the work may be satisfactorily carried on, and the staff should be increased. I know that the receipts by the patent office are greatly in excess of the expenditures. Apparently this is one department of government which carries itself. I have not the figures here, but I think I am safe in saying that the surplus of receipts over expenditures averages over $200,000 a year.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
I am glad to be able to assure my hon. friend that this matter is being looked into. One of the first things I found in my department was that the staff of the patent office was totally inadequate and that the office itself was in most undesirable surroundings. The Department of National Defence is moving out of the Woods building and the annex, now known as the Canada building, and the patent office is to be moved there. Some floors are already available, and I have taken steps to have some of the branches of the patent office, now in outlying buildings, moved to the Canada building. I am hoping that in a short time we shall be able to have the whole patent office installed in that building.
Supply-Secretary of Stale

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
Does the minister
expect to have any difficulty in obtaining personnel for the department?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I suppose this matter should be taken up under the item dealing with the patent office, but I can say that there has been difficulty in securing staff. Just the other day we told two applicants that we had positions for them, but in the meantime they had secured other employment. When we are in the enlarged quarters to which we intend to move it will be possible to fill positions without having applicants wait and possibly secure other positions in the meantime. In that way we shall be more likely to secure the necessary staff to undertake the work.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
Has the government given
consideration to the establishment of a national library for Canada? I do not know whether this comes under the minister's department; I am not sure what department it would come under, but there seems to be a general demand for a national library for Canada.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
That
question is, I think, properly asked here. We have no national library, but I have received a great many representations from organizations from one end of Canada to the other as to the desirability of organizing a national library for Canada, The brief submitted was, I thought, very reasonable. They did not suggest that we should spend one or two million dollars at the outset in putting up a building, but that a committee be appointed, consisting of one librarian and a small staff, who would find out and catalogue from the libraries of this country what books are available to assist students, and from that gradually work up to a national library and a building which would probably be situated in Ottawa. At the present time all Canadian publications are filed with the library of parliament, and that is not altogether a suitable place. I am having the matter considered at the present time, and I think a committee of the library of parliament is also giving the matter consideration to find out the best step to take first.

367.	Citizenship registration branch, $74,775.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: How many citizenship certificates have been issued to date; how many for $1, and how many for $5?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
We had certificates issued under the previous act. On the first of January the number of naturalization certificates issued was 3,178; certificates in proof of citizenship, 2,816; certificates granted to aliens and sent to the courts, 4,085; certificates issued in the French language, 250; making a total of 10,329. Those are the cases that have actually been investigated and dealt with. When an application for citizenship is received the certificate does

Supply-Secretary of State
not issue automatically; there has to be some investigation. It will be noted from the above figures that 2.816 certificates of proof of citizenship have actually been issued. The applications number 5.493, which leaves approximately 2,600 applications pending.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Would these be natural-born Canadians?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Yes. Certificates in proof are issued to those who are already Canadian citizens.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Apparently nobody is bothering very much about it.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I have had complaints as to the length of time it takes, not only after the application has been put in, but to get the application form sent to the applicant. Could something not be done to shorten the time? It may be just a matter of routine.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: There was delay earlier in the year because we had to change the type of form. The amount charged for the certificate was reduced and various amendments were made to make the form more convenient to the applicant. This meant that the forms had to be changed, and there was some delay on that account. We now endeavour to keep all the clerks of the courts supplied with application forms so that they can supply them to any applicants in their own locality.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: All too often we forget the officials who do the hard toil in our departments. I want to pay my tribute to the under-secretary for naturalization, both the present gentleman and his predecessor. Their efficiency is marked and their courtesy could not be beat even by a cabinet minister. I am happy to pay my tribute to them.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Under item 367 we are asked to vote $74,775 for the citizenship registration branch; and a few items below, in item 373, we are asked to vote $79,300 for the citizenship branch. What are the functions of the citizenship registration branch and what are the functions of the citizenship branch? Do these branches overlap? If so, is consideration being given to bringing them together?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
The
citizenship registration branch is the old naturalization branch. We changed the name to correspond with the Citizenship Act. It carries on the same functions it performed before, that of issung certificates to citizens. The citizenship branch mentioned in item 373 is the department that looks after education
and training for citizenship. It is working in conjunction with the provinces to bring the new arrivals of this country up to a common standard of education that will be satisfactory to the judges before whom they appear to become citizens.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Which is the branch that issues a certificate to a man or a woman who is already a Canadian citizen?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
The
citizenship registration branch.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
In what position is the application for citizenship of Igor Gouzenko?
I take it that his letters of denization which make him a British subject have been given. I understand that the next step is to make application to become a Canadian citizen. Because of the public interest in the matter, and because it was discussed in the house before, can the minister indicate whether or not application has actually been made?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: In other words, although letters of denization creating him a British subject have been made by statute, there is apparently no short-cut being made to make him a Canadian citizen.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: No. The regulations for citizenship are set out by statute, and we have no powers of shortening the periods that are provided by statute.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I mentioned the $5 and the $1 certificates. Can the minister tell us whether any refund has been made to those who paid $5?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24

speechtext: It should not be necessary.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: It should not be necessary, no; I can check into that.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: There is a good deal of uncertainty in some parts of the country regarding the necessity of having a citizenship certificate. Suppose a person were born in Canada or had been naturalized for a long time; would there be any difficulty in his obtaining the privilege of voting if he did not happen to have his citizenship paper? Does he have that right because of the standing he had before this citizenship paper business came into effect?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: There is no need for any Canadian citizen to have a certificate to prove his citizenship. He is entitled to secure such a certificate if he requires it. If he has been naturalized or was born in Canada, under the provisions of the Citizenship Act he is a Canadian citizen and requires no certificate, but he is entitled to have one if he wishes to secure it.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Does this branch exercise any control over the design of trade marks similar to the control which, I believe, is exercised by the college of heralds in England?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: It exercises control over the design that is registered, but I do not think it corresponds with the college of heralds in England. The college of heralds has a function quite different from any commercial function.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Does the college of heralds not have to pass on the design of all trade marks in Great Britain? Does the minister's branch exercise control over a trade mark which is submitted? Does it check on the various insignia which might be inscribed or included in the trade mark?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
I do not know the full duties of the college of heralds in England, but, of course, there is a tax on the use of heraldic designs in Great Britain which does not exist in this country. If anybody wants to use a trade mark or a design without registering it he is perfectly at liberty to do so, so long as he is not

Supply-Secretary of State
infringing on one already registered. If persons wish to register a trade mark they register it with this branch.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: The design of a trade mark has to be approved, and no insignia can be included in that design which was not approved by this branch if application was made to the branch to register the trade mark. Is that correct?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I should like to speak about the accommodation of the trade marks branch. My experience has been that they operate their offices in an efficient manner. They have a system of cross-checking and double cross-checking, and they seem to be going at it in a businesslike way. But in my attendances at their offices I have noticed that they have only about three offices and a public hall in a building on Queen street. I should think that close to their offices other office space should be available. With all their inconveniences they do an extremely good job. I really believe that the time has come to make more space available to them. I noticed that the public office is really a private office used by several stenographers and one of the department heads. It cannot be entirely satisfactory to those who go there to make searches or to the staff itself.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24

speechtext: Why is the trade marks branch kept separate from the copyright and industrial design divisions, which is item 376? As I understand it, these matters all come under the Unfair Competition Act. Is there a differentiation between trade marks, copyright and industrial designs?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Yes. Industrial designs do not come under the Unfair Competition Act, and that is why they are separate.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: What about copyrights?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Copyrights do.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: In this trade marks branch I note that the salaries are $21,600, and that the salaries for temporary assistance are $18,150 approximately, so that they are almost the same for the permanent staff and the temporary staff. Does "temporary assistance" refer to that portion of the civil service staff which has not yet been made permanent?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: It does not apply merely to persons taken on for shorter periods of time?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: No. It means that the permanent establishment has not been built up beyond the figures shown in this case, which is eleven. We have temporary employees in addition to that.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
It is the policy of the government that a certain portion of the staff of each department shall be temporary.
Supply-Secretary oj State

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I believe the idea was to keep it around ten per cent. Evidently it is much more than that in this instance. I take it that there are more temporaries in this branch than there are members of the permanent staff, because they would likely be the lower-paid staff. 'Since the total of both salaries is in each case almost the same, there would seem to be just as many temporaries as there are permanent, or more. I suggest that in the future the number of temporaries should be given as well as the number of permanents, so that we shall know exactly how many persons are employed in the branch.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Do I take it that the trade marks branch is part and parcel of the accommodation provided for the patent office?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: No. It has a separate office of its own at the present time.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: It has its own office?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Is further accommodation provided for the trade marks branch?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
