subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I cannot say until we find out what the Department of Public Works can do for us. I am not sure how much space the patent office will require in the Canada building. If we had additional available space it would be convenient to have all our offices in close contact.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Is the trade marks office separate from the patent office?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Yes.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: So far as administration and records are concerned?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Yes.

Item agreed to.
370.	Bureau for translations, $503,505.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: There is an item here of over half a million dollars, there being an increase of over $11,000 as compared with last year. Would the minister give a little sketch of the work of this particular bureau and at the same time account for the increase? When I hear what he has to say I may have another question to direct to him.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: The bureau for translations provides all the translators for the various departments of government. There is some increase from the previous year. Whereas it was $492,000 last year, this year it is $503,000, and most of that increase is due to salary increases.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I take it that practically the whole item is devoted to salaries of translators. Is that a fact? What languages are handled besides English and French?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I could not enumerate all the languages, but we have translators who can translate in most languages in current use.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Has any work been done by this particular group of translators for the censorship branch of the customs end of the Department of National Revenue? Do other departments submit to this particular branch various works for translations from time to time?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: This division provides translators. In many cases they are attached to other government departments, but they are carried and financed through the bureau for translations, although they may be regularly attached to one of the departments of government.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Would I be safe in saying that the censorship branch has no translators of its own but submits work to this particular department?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I would not say it submits its work. I would have to get the details of the particular branch, but the chances are that a translator from this bureau is attached to the censorship branch.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: I notice that this year there are no supervisors of technical translations, but there are ten for 1947-48 and there were twenty parliamentary translators for 1946-47 and twenty-two for 1947-48. Would the minister explain the difference between a technical translator and a parliamentary translator, and why it is necessary to add ten next year and none this year? There are head translators, principal translators and senior translators. What are the functions of all these different translators?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Of course the functions of the translators are to translate.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
Yes, I understand that.
That is a rather smart remark. But what is the difference between a technical translator and a parliamentary translator? I know they are all to translate. But why not call them all translators? -

Supply-Secretary of State

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
The
parliamentary translators are those who are employed in the House of Commons, translating parliamentary papers at the House of Commons. This bureau provides all the translators required in the government service. The supervisors are those who have been put in a supervisory position to look after those who are in the junior positions.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: What is a technical translator?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
He is
one who translates technical documents, such as those which come from foreign countries to the patent office; for example those that come from Germany, or those in Spanish.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Why is it you need them for next year but did not need them for this year? Were there no technical documents to translate in the past?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: What is a senior translator?

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
Shall the
item carry?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext: Would it be a fair statement to make that if we had bilingual administrative officers many of these ninety-six translators would not be necessary?

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
No, I
would not think that would be a fair inference at all, because a great many of these translators are doing just routine work-translating documents in a routine way-which a senior official would not be handling.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
That is exactly what I
mean. If they are doing routine work on correspondence and things like that, if there were bilingual officers to look after that routine correspondence which comes in in French, for instance, or in English, and those officers were able to handle both French and English it would not be necessary to have as many translators in that department, and the routine would be handled much faster.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
In some
cases it would reduce the number by a small amount.

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
The minister has not
answered my question. Might I suggest that it might have been a good idea if he had had his technical advisers in front of him. They might have been able to tell us what technical translators are for.
Mr. MhcINNIS:	May I ask the minister-

subtopic: MB. GKAYDON-REFEBENCE TO REMARKS MADE IN DEBATE ON JUNE 24
speechtext:
He has not answered my
question yet.

-what is the difference
between supervisors of technical translation and head translators? I notice that there are ten supervisors of technical translation this year and there were not any last year. On the other hand, there were fourteen head translators last year and there are only three this year.
I cannot tell. I can secure that information but I presume that is a-
Reshuffle.
-reclassification by the civil service commission. I can get that information for my hon. friend, but I cannot give it at the moment.

Item agreed to.
S71. Canada Temperance Act, $4,500.
What is the purpose of this item? Why is there a $2,000 increase this year? Is the act being applied now? If so, where?

The Canada Temperance Act applies in a few places in Canada. The cost of administration is really the cost of having prosecutions in those centres where we are in charge of administering the act. I may say the fines which have been secured fairly well offset the cost of that branch to the department, but they go into the eon-solidated revenue fund.	[DOT]
Why are no details given of this item in the same way as they are given with regard to other items? It is not marked statutory. There is just a blank there.
The less said about it, the better.

Because it is only a sum of money which is voted as a contingency in case it is needed for the coming year. It is to pay the fees of administering the act if any cases came up which require the engaging of counsel. We have not any permanent staff engaged in doing that work.
Of the amount which was voted last year for doing that work, how much was paid out?
Expenditures for 1946-47, $6,250.

Item agreed to.
372. Bankruptcy Act administration, $32,960.

How many petitions in bankruptcy were filed last year, and how many the year before?

Supply-Secretary oj State
I shall have to get that information for my hon. friend.

Item agreed to.
ST3. Citizenship branch, $79,300.
If I understood the minister correctly, he told us, under item 369, that the citizenship branch looked after education and training for citizenship.
No.
Looked after education and training of people who had acquired citizenship.
No. I should like to explain that.
I did not understand it.
Education comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces.
I understand that. Is this education and training of people who apply to become citizens or of people who have received certificates of citizenship?

No. This branch is working in conjunction with the provinces to provide that those people who come to this country and wish to become naturalized, or are eligible to become naturalized. They should receive some training in citizenship so that they will be able to pass the examinations they are faced with when they appear before the judge in court. For example, I have a letter which I received just a few days ago from a judge out west in which he says that of nineteen applicants there was only one who had even the foggiest idea of what citizenship in this country meant, and he points out the necessity of having some training in citizenship for newcomers to this country. A month or two ago I held a meeting with representatives of the departments of education of all the provinces, with the exception of Ontario and Quebec. We drew up a tentative plan whereby the provinces would undertake to do a certain amount of training, and we were investigating in what way we could assist by providing them with material which would enable them to have a standard course of education throughout the whole country.

In the details on page 219 of the estimates, I notice that there is a director of this branch who gets So,400; a clerk, grade 4, who gets $2,004; then there is temporary assistance, $54,696. Can the minister give us a break-down of how it is proposed to spend that money?

This is, of course, a new branch which was organized
I Mr. Hazen.]
shortly before the first of this year when the Citizenship Act came into force, with the result that we took on a temporary staff. Only the two permanent employees were in the branch, and they were permanent because they had been permanent government employees prior to being moved over to the citizenship branch. The staff is now about twenty. They examine foreign language newspapers and keep in touch with the various organizations which can assist in citizenship training throughout the country. We have many calls from various foreign groups in the country to provide speakers to address them and give them talks on citizenship in Canada.
Last year we voted $34,000 for this purpose. Is that amount all paid in wages or salaries to temporary staff, or is some of it expended in other ways?

That
$34,000 was for the previous year. It is $54,000 this year.
I am asking whether it was all expended on wages or salaries, or was some of it for that purpose, and some of it for something else?
It was all for wages and salaries.
Were all those wages and salaries, or practically all, paid here in Ottawa to people employed here, or were they paid in other provinces?
It was all paid here.

What is the basis of temporary assistance? I understand1 that in the Post Office Department-and certainly in my city it is this way-ten per cent of the staff is kept permanently on the temporary list. In other words of the total complement of personnel ten per cent is always temporary. Is there a rule of that kind which runs through all government departments, and in particular the Department of the Secretary of State? What is the nature of this temporary employment? How long have these people who are drawing temporary assistants' pay this year been with the department? Perhaps the minister can tell us the personal history of employment of those people, so that we might have some idea of the situation. Then, are any of the temporary help employed by the minister's department or, to his knowledge other departments of government, either permanently or temporarily employed by other departments of governmert?

Supply-Secretary oj State
Prior to the war, it was the custom-and it has been carried on since-to have a certain percentage of each staff on the temporary list, so that if the work declined the staff could be reduced.
How does that work out in the minister's department?

During the war the number of temporaries increased tremendously. We had the veterans preference, of course, and practically no permanent appointments were made during the war. The result is that we have in all departments a large number of temporaries who could not be made permanent during the war and, if there are no veterans available, will be eligible for permanent appointment to take over the positions they are now occupying.

That answers only part of my question. In other words, this matter of temporary assistants is an outgrowth of war conditions?
' Mr. GIBSON (Hamilton West): I should say that it is, to some extent.
I should like to know what it is to the full extent.

In any department the permanent staff is set at a certain number. If additional employees are required, temporary employees can be secured. But the department is still limited to the original number of permanent employees, unless the permanent establishment of the department is increased. Until that permanent establishment has been set, the department cannot, of course, appoint permanent employees to fill positions.

How long is it before the minister can obtain from his colleagues permission to put temporary staff on the permanent list? Does it run into two years, five years or ten years? I have come across cases in the Post Office Department where it runs into many years. What has been the experience in this department with respect to temporary assistants who this year will draw $54,000? How long have those individuals been with the department, and how long have they been temporary?
This is a new branch, of course, which has just been set up.
What about the minister's department?

In the other departments, many of them have been 83166-297J
in for five or six, or perhaps seven or eight years. That, of course, is due largely to war conditions. I believe it was customary before the war that a person would not remain temporary for more than five or six years, if he was giving good service. Then a vacancy would occur; someone would retire, and there would be an opportunity for a temporary employee to be absorbed into the permanent establishment. The civil service commission has been making a survey of various government departments to find out what the permanent establishments should be. It is all being revised at the present time.
May I have an answer to my last question? Are some of the minister's temporary help also employed in other departments?
I do not understand the question.

Let us suppose a man has a post with the civil service in one department. Can he do temporary work in the minister's department or in some other department; or can a man who has not a full-time job with any department be on the temporary list of several departments of government?
He can fill only one position at one time. He cannot have two positions at the same time.
It is quite possible that a man may fill in, in one department for part of the year, and then may go to another department; does that not happen?
That happens all the time, yes.
How many of the new $5 Canadian citizenship certificates have been issued up to date?
It is one dollar.

I gave that information a few minutes ago. There have been actually issued this year 2.816 certificates of proof of citizenship. However, there are many applications now under consideration which have not been dealt with.

In the list of temporary assistants, are there any employees who did not work for the government until they were taken over by the Department of the Secretary of State? If so, how many? Have all these so-called temporary assistants already been employed in other departments of government and, within the last year or so, been absorbed by this department?
Supply-Secretary of Stale
I cannot give that information, but perhaps I can secure it. We secure employees through the civil service commission, but I have no record of what they were doing before that.

If there are pools of unabsorbed temporary assistants in the different departments of government, I want to know whether or not the Department of the Secretary of State hires, through the civil service commission, individual temporary assistants, or whether they are absorbed from other departments?
If my department has a vacancy we apply to the civil service commission and they make an appointment. We do not hire direct.

How many employees in the minister's department who are now temporary have been there for more than five or six years? I understand that some departments have a habit of keeping employees a great many years on a temporary status. I do not believe the minister's department is one of the worst offenders in this respect. However I am wondering how many employees in his department who have served there for five or six years or more are still temporary.
I have not that information now, but I can get it. Of course a great many temporaries who came in during the war are still temporary.

I understood the minister to say a few minutes ago, in connection with the citizenship branch, that he had had a conference with representatives from a number of the other provinces about the work to be done. He added that that conference did not include Ontario and Quebec. I should like to ask him why Ontario and Quebec were not included. This was not a matter of interprovincial arrangements about taxation or anything like that; it had to do with the education of our future citizens.

I wrote to all the ministers of education in the provinces suggesting that this conference be held. Colonel Drew replied that he considered the facilities of Ontario were quite capable of providing whatever standard of education it was felt the immigrant should receive and that he did not consider it necessary to be represented at the conference. Premier Duplessis sent a telegram a few days before the conference stating that Quebec would not be represented. Apart from those two cases, all the other provinces were represented.
	'

The minister gave us the number of citizenship applications which had been made and for which the SI fee was paid, but I should like to know in how many cases the $5 fee was paid and whether this has been refunded?
That would be included in the number of those who had applied for certificates in proof of citizenship.
The number the minister gave would include the $5 applications?
No. The $5 applications are made by those being naturalized for the first time.
When the citizenship bill first came down it provided for a fee of $5. How many applied under that and paid the S5 which will have to be refunded?

The
original bill provided that the applicant should pay $5, either for naturalization, or a certificate in proof of citizenship. With the consent of parliament we reduced the fee for a certifi-' cate in proof of citizenship to $1. Certificates in proof of citizenship were issued to a few applicants before the fee was reduced, but I have not the number. They would be entitled to have a refund of the extra S4.
Has the $4 already been refunded?
I cannot say whether it has been, but it is due and it will be refunded.

There are a great number of people in this country who have oome from other countries. During the

Supply-Secretary of State
war very few people were naturalized and those of enemy nationality could not be naturalized. We are trying to raise the standard of education of those whom we receive as citizens. At one time a man could go before a judge, and if he could speak the English or the French language he was granted a certificate practically automatically. We sent out a letter to judges all across the country asking their opinions as to what should be the minimum standard of education or training for these applicants. We received some most interesting letters from judges all over the country. Those were summarized. The general opinion was that 'the person being naturalized should at least be able to read a daily paper printed either in English or in French, so that he would not 'have to rely .upon a foreign language paper. We should like, if possible, to get these applicants up to a standard whereby they would know something about our ideas of democracy and our way of life.
Have any schools been opened for that purpose? Where is the money being spent?
That is what we were discussing with the provinces. It is hoped to be able to build up classes in the various provinces to give instructions to these new Canadians.

The new Canadians who come here at the present time will have to go on the land and they will be scattered all over the country. How could you have a class in one central area for those people? They will not attend such a class or, if they do, it will be at considerable expense to someone because they will not have the funds themselves. I think it is a waste of money.

I should like to bring up the matter I brought up before. Here is a vote of $54,000 for temporary assistance in this branch. The total estimates are $1,228,000, of which $429,000 is for temporary assistance. Yet we never get an itemized account.

I wish to refer again to the education given to these new citizens. The minister said that he had received quite a few letters from judges throughout the country complaining about the standard of education, and he went on to indicate that in his opinion they should be able to read newspapers. I am sure there are some of us here who cannot read newspapers and get any sense out of them.
You might say the same thing about Hansard.

I did not want to appear personal, so I did not make that reference. I know personally where people have come before a judge and he has said to them, "You cannot read English; you will have to postpone your application." Where are those people to go? The minister has indicated that there have been some conversations with the provinces, but have any schools been opened for these people to attend? I do not suppose it is expected that they will attend the public schools. Are you expecting that a person of forty or fifty years of age will go through the school and take a course in English literature or something of that kind? It seems to me that the minister is going into something which will entail a considerable amount of money if any results are to be obtained. I am not belittling the idea that these people should be educated in the English language before they are allowed citizenship, but I am just wondering how the money will be spent.
Classes have been conducted in some cities for many years.
What is the procedure in connection with those classes?
They are being held in normal schools. For instance, in Toronto they had a successful class which used to meet in one of the normal schools. Various instructors would come there to instruct.
Would attendance be compulsory, and would they pay for tuition?

Not at all. Those who wished to attend were permitted to attend. That was provided by the departments of education in the various provinces, and it is hoped that these classes will be extended. It may be necessary to have teachers travel to various centres and hold classes once a week or so many times a month, or whatever the provinces can arrange. We do want them to get some instruction.
Will the schools set up by the provinces be assisted by a dominion grant?

They wrould not likely get a government grant, although I should not be too sure about that because nothing has been arranged with the provinces on that point. The matter is under consideration. We will assist them as far as we can in providing textbooks.

The director of the branch is getting an increase of over $2,000. Is a change being made there?
Supply-Secretary of State
What was actually spent last year?
We actually spent in 1946-47, 858,006.
Is a new director being appointed?

The director was a permanent civil servant, in the Department of Agriculture. During the war he was given other duties and was drawing the war duties supplement in addition to his permanent salary from the Department of Agriculture. Now that he is with this branch his salary as a permanent civil servant is $5,400.
What are his qualifications for the position? It seems to be a senior position.

He is a man who has had overseas service. He has had wide experience in public service. I think he is president of the agricultural federation of Canada. He has given very good service in organizing this citizenship branch, and that is the chief function of his division.

I asked the minister before whether there were any employees of other departments who were on his temporary staff. The minister now mentions that during the war years this particular gentleman was seconded from the Department of Agriculture, whether on part time or full time-
On full time.
-and that he drew the war duties supplement and now is being raised to a more adequate salary; is that the story?

No. He was drawing his salary as a permanent employee of the Department of Agriculture. Then he was transferred or lent to another department, and for those new duties he received the war duties supplement.

That was the question I asked, whether there were any employees from one department of government who became temporary assistants in another department and therefore drew 'remuneration from two departments? The war may have led to unusual and necessary situations of that kind. What I am asking is, are there any employees in the year 1947 in one department of government who are lent or seconded or otherwise giving their services to another department and being paid therefor by two departments?

No
employee is being paid by two departments. This employee was permanently employed by the Department of Agriculture at the salary rate set for his duties. When he was doing temporary work in another department he was paid his regular rate of salary, plus the war duties supplement to which he was entitled. He has now been transferred to the Department of Secretary of State and draws his salary from this department at this rate.

I do not know anything about the gentleman, how able he is or otherwise. I do not know whether he is young or elderly, but his total remuneration in 1946-47, even with the war duties supplement, was $3,240.
No; that was his permanent salary. His war duties supplement was in addition to that.
How much would his war duties supplement be, approximately?
To bring it up to $5,400, and when he was given a permanent appointment in the citizenship branch he was given what he was drawing before.

He must have been
getting a very large war duties supplement.

He was
doing important work.

The minister said that
the citizenship branch proposes to publish certain text books which will be suitable for new Canadians. There is an item here of $8,000 for printing, but I do not suppose that would cover these textbooks. How is it proposed to cover the cost of the textbooks? Have any textbooks been printed so far?

All we
have done so far is to have some pamphlets printed. As I said before, education is within the jurisdiction of the provinces, and all this has to be worked out in conjunction with the provinces.

Have the clerks of the
superior courts of the province of Quebec been provided with forms in the French language for applicants for citizenship certificates?

If they
have not got them I will see that they get them. We have had application forms printed in the French language for that purpose.

They have been waiting
for them for six months.

Sup-ply-Secretary of State

Has the minister a
break-down by provinces and by district courts of the number of applications for certificates that have been refused?
Applications for naturalization?
Yes.

I have
not got that, but possibly it can be secured.

I should like to get
that from the department.
I will try to get it.

A good many people came to this country as adults and now they wish to make application for citizenship. They appear in the district court before the district court judge and very often they feel intimidated by the very atmosphere of the court. Sometimes they report to me that they went into the courtroom, which they usually associate with crime, and they were so completely upset by their surroundings and the number of questions fired at them that they became confused and did not really understand the questions which were being asked. Could there not be some uniformity of examination by the judges? Otherwise there are bound to be differences of opinion among the judges as to the applicant's knowledge of his responsibilities as a citizen. Is any textbook prepared similar to the one which is used in the United States? They have a similar department over there. Last year I understood from the then secretary of state that it was the intention of the department to publish a number of these booklets and make them available to persons who are making application. The waiting period in Canada is quite long. When they make application such a textbook should be placed in their hands. Such a textbook would go a long way toward showing them what their responsibilities and rights are in a democratic state. Has such a textbook been prepared?

With reference to the first question, I mentioned a few minutes ago that we had circularized all the judges in Canada to find out if we could adopt a common standard throughout the country. I quite realize, as the hon. member has said, that standards vary in various localities according to the personality of the judge, and the judge himself has, of course, the final decision. We received replies from the judges across the country as to what they thought should be a common standard. Those
were summarized, and we have sent copies out to the judges so that they will have it, not as instructions from our department, but as a summary of the advice received from the judges themselves. In that way we hope to have more or less a common Standard adopted throughout the counfry.
The first publication that we are getting out I hope to have ready early in July, which will be available to be given to newcomers to this country when they arrive. We got one out in Polish which we gave to the Polish soldiers when they came. It is not as elaborate as the one which is used in the United Statps at the present time. We hope to make progress and to have better publications as time goes on.

I know
there are French citizenship certificates and English ones, but I should like to know from the minister whether his department has considered issuing bilingual certificates.

Yes, that has been given careful consideration, but there is so much on the certificate, both on the front and on the back of it, that it was felt it would be confusing to an applicant coming to this country, who perhaps knows only one language, either French or English, to receive the certificate partly in a language which he does not understand. Consequently it was felt that it would be better to give him a certificate in either the French or the English language, whichever was the language that he had acquired while in this country.
What if he does not know either the English or the French language?
Then he is not qualified for citizenship.

For purposes of travelling, would it not be preferable to have both the French and the English language on the same certificate as is done with passports, because an English person having an English certificate and going to France would find that they could not read the English language, and conversely a French-speaking Canadian with a French certificate going to England would be embarrassed by the fact that the certificate is not in English.
Of course a citizenship certificate is not a passport; it is not intended for the purpose of being used as a passport.
For identification purposes.
Yes.

Some time ago I asked the minister whether he would consider having
Supply-Secretary of State

the citizenship certificate printed in a form similar to that which is used for birth certificates in Ontario. He said that he would consider the matter. Has he given any further consideration with respect to this?

I took the matter up, but I received a reply on the costs from the company which manufactures these only about two or three days ago. I have not had time yet to give much consideration as to whether it would be desirable at this time to do that or not.

As I pointed out before, a big certificate would be fine perhaps for someone who values this kind of thing to keep in his home or in some other place; but when he wants to use it for the purpose of identification or for some other purpose, I believe that custom and usage have brought these things down to rather small dimensions. I think a size of the birth certificate which I hold in my hand would be more helpful, because when an individual wishes to go across the border or to use it for some other purpose he will find that a certificate of this size would fit into a billfold quite easily. The people of Ontario have found these eminently satisfactory.
Is that a photostatic copy of the original?
This is a birth certificate af one of my own children. I brought it to the minister's attention some time ago to indicate the type of certificate it is.

There is one disadvantage about having that type of certificate. It is so easily carried that it can be easily lost. There would be the danger of a certificate being carried by people being lost, which might be of value to people into whose hands we would not want it to fall. Consequently it might be better to have certificates in a larger form which could not so easily be carried or so easily lost.

Some time ago during this session the minister told the house that each year the patent office had a substantial surplus which was transferred to the consolidated revenue fund. It would be appreciated if he would enlarge upon this matter and tell us what progress is being made in that regard.

This
really shows the disadvantage of going from item to item. The administration of the Secretary of State's office was discussed at the opening of the session tonight, and I said that we expected to move into the building which has been vacated by the Department of National Defence. I am hoping to have my patent division in there' within the next week or two.

In connection with patents which were issued before the war and in connection with certain patents that had to be held up because of the war and because of the lack of material during the war which prevented the manufacture and development of these patents, what procedure has a person to go through in order to have an extension of that patent? It seems to me unfair that certain people should have been held up and have not had time within the life of the patent to develop it. Is there not some way whereby that can be corrected, so that they can go to a court of law or to some such place in order to have the matter adjudicated and bring witnesses and so on? Is something being done about that?

All that can be done by an act of parliament. One holder of a patent this year made application for an extension of his patent and parliament did not see fit to grant it. I do not think parliament as a whole has 'looked favourably on extensions of patents.

What about the fairness of it? I was wondering whether the minister contemplated some provision whereby patents could be reviewed by courts instead of having to come to parliament where the proper witnesses cannot be brought to testify?
That is not under contemplation.

During the war the archives staff was cut down materially. We have some representatives in France looking up material, and that office had been closed. The staff is now being brought up to usual strength again.

What is being done in regard to the archives? I have been told on numerous occasions that we should consider more seriously the position of the archives branch of our government and that we might do more than we are doing, even at greater expense. The reason there may be a certain timeliness in that suggestion is that many historical documents and other treasures which would ordinarily find a safe resting place in the national archives are being sold to other bodies and even outside the country. Wpuld the minister sa.y a word or two in that regard and indicate whether any development is planned in the near future?

There was a recommendation before the war that the building itself should be enlarged, but that has not been possible up to the present time. The staff of the archives are doing what they can to keep up to date with the material. They are making copies of all material dealing with the early history of the country. I do not believe that we have enough money to buy as much of the material that is now available as we should. It is a matter in which I intend to take some interest. This year we are really just carrying along on the 83166-298
routine we have followed in previous years, and it is possible that we should do more than we are doing at the present time.
Last year, for temporary assistance, there was $14,000 odd and this year there as an estimate of $36,000 odd. Can the minister explain the great increas''?
Staffs wb.e cut down tremendously during the war, and the work of the archives both overseas and in this country was greatly curtailed. We are now trying to catch up.
Is there any reason why, if the staff is being increased, it should be increased on a temporary rather than on a permanent basis?

Until the positions are established as permanent and until we know that there are no veterans available-some of these temporaries were not overseas-it is not considered advisable to make them permanent.

When did the minister last have a report on the general policy of the archives branch? I do not mean from the director general, but a report on what the archives should consist of. speakeroldname: Hon. ALPHONSE FOURNIER (Minister of Public Works):
speechtext: This is a revote of $52,000 from last year to provide for the erection of a new public building to accommodate all the public services at Belleville. The existing public building erected in 1880 no longer provides sufficient space for the postal and customs business, and the erection of a new building is strongly recommended. This is only the first vote toward the construction of that building, for the preparation of plans and specifications. The building itself will cost far more than that. We shall know only when the tenders come in what the amount will be.
Is it the intention to have all the various federal branches in the one building?

I will give the hon. member every department which will be accommodated in this building: income tax division, unemployment insurance commission, trade and commerce, post office, agriculture, health and welfare, labour, Royal Canadian Mounted Police, customs, and the janitor's quarters.
I do not see anything in the estimates this year for a new federal building for Peterborough, which was promised us away back about 1900.
What year?
About 1900.

I do not know what was proposed in 1900, but I do know that we are studying the possibility of having a new building in Peterborough, We are making a survey of every town and city in the country as to the needs of the different departments for the erection of new buildings. I will look into the Peterborough case and do my utmost to give the hon. gentleman satisfaction.

The customs house there has been overcrowded for some years, and it is awkward now for the officials of the customs house to work there. At the post office extra space has to be rented not just once a year but, I think, more than once a year, and the postmaster has had to give up some of the space in his office in order to make more room in the lobby of the post office for people to come in and post their letters. The lobby of the post office in Peterborough, a city of 35,000, is no larger, I think, than the post office in Lakefield, which has a population of only 1,600. I may say also that the washroom in the post office for the men is down in the basement and it is unsanitary and very small.
What is this $100,000 revote for Hamilton for?

A revote of
$100,000 toward the purchase of a site and the erection thereon of an office building to provide accommodation for the Department of Veterans Affairs and the unemployment insurance commission in Hamilton. The cost of the proposed building is not known; it will run to about $500,000. That is just an estimate.

Whereabouts is it being
built?

I am told that
they are considering the old collegiate site.

Might I suggest that
the proposed revision of the income tax departments throughout Canada, if they do a good job, will make available plenty of room in the present federal building, and it will not be necessary to spend half a million dollars on additional public buildings in Hamilton. I am not one of those who advocate putting up public buildings all over the country. What I think we should do is attempt to cut down on these expenditures.
The hon. member is a great help to me.

If you erect the building
you will have to keep it in repair at a great cost to the taxpayers of this country. I do not want the minister to put any post offices in my riding or make any additional grants in the form of public expenditure so far as public buildings are concerned. I think we have too many now.

That is good
news.

With regard to accommodation for the Department of Trade and Commerce, revote $25,500, total of $31,000, a reduction of $4,000, will the minister please tell us what that is?

This is a revote of $25,000 for the construction of a building requested by the Department of Trade and Commerce to provide accommodation for their weights and measures inspection service at Calgary; to provide facilities for this service, particularly; for oil truck calibration is important in the Calgary district owing to its proximity to the Turner valley oil fields. The district inspector of the weights and measures section service at Calgary reports that a garage on Tenth avenue in which his department has installed a 50-gallon calibrating tank has been sold, and that he is expecting notice to vacate at any time. No other suitable accommodation is available for rental in Calgary. The estimated cost of the site is $1,375; the new building, $27,000; grading and sidewalks, $500; supervision, $1,000; contingencies, $2,625. We expect to spend that amount this year. W'e expect to spend the amount of $31,000 on that building for weights and measures. I have given the break-down of what we think the site will cost, the building, the grading and sidewalks, the supervision and so forth.
Where is it?
On the 14th of November the government-
That is a date, not the address.

I will give exactly what it is; lots 21, 22; block 106, plan C, section 15 on the northwest corner of First street east and Fifteenth avenue. That is the exact location where we are to purchase the site.
What I am wondering about is this: may I say this is within the constituency of the hon. member for Calgary East.
I noticed that.

It is not of my bailiwick. Recently the government has had a tremendous building turned over to it. By "tremendous" I mean it must be
two or three hundred feet long, four or five stories high and at least 100 feet in depth, which was occupied by military district 13; that is now turned back. I have noticed in the newspapers that certain government departments are moving into this building. It is an immense building. Has the minister made any sort of survey to find out whether this building could not easily accommodate a little thing like a weights and measures department without new construction at the corner of Fifteenth avenue and First street east?

The building the hon. member mentions is rented by National Defence. When they are through using that building they turn it over to War Assets Corporation, but Public Works has priority on these buildings which are turned over to War Assets Corporation. We have not heard that this building has as yet been vacated or released to War Assets Corporation. I am told by my officials that this building for weights and measures is a special sort of building which we could not transform into an office building erected for office space.

With respect,
I do not think the answer of the minister is quite good enough. Surely this government which owns buildings in the city of Calgary-
I do not care what department it is in-is not going to have War Assets Corporation sell it to someone if this same government has another department which can occupy it.
They will not do that if we need it, because it will have to be offered to Public Works.

You do need it. If the minister followed the newspapers recently he will find that a number of departments of government have already moved into this building to which I am referring. I do not know what weights and measures need. I know they require a weigh scale and certified weights and that sort of thing; but this is really a big place, about two or three times the size of this chamber, and there is a tremendous amount of space there. I am quite sure that the person who is going to sell the lot will enjoy it, but what I am trying to do is to suggest some sort of economy even in my own city. Most people ask for expenditures.
This is not in your riding.
No, two blocks out.

Don't worry about that.
Supply-Public Works

What I am seeking to do is to find a bit of economy in the picture where the thing seems to be written plainly on the wall that you can use this accommodation for perhaps a number of other departments in that city.

The only answer I can give is to read the report of our resident architect in Calgary who advises us on these matters. He says:
I do not consider it possible under existing conditions to obtain space for the calibration service in an existing building. I recommend that a new building be provided in the central part of Calgary as near the customs building as possible for this service, and if necessary the electricity and gas inspection service as well.
I am further informed that the city is selling these lots I mentioned a moment ago for the amount of $1,375. I do not know; perhaps my hon. friend could advise me, but the architect is the only man upon whom I can rely as to the conditions and the kind of building that is needed. The request comes from the Department of Trade and Commerce to Public Works. They tell us what kind of building they will require, and the request is sent to the resident architect who ' makes a survey and advises the department as to what should be done. Perhaps he is all wrong; I do not know. Personally I think he is right, though he may be making a mistake. I do not know, however, that I can convince the Department of Trade and Commerce that they should try to turn over another building for the purpose for which they need this special building. The hon. member may know' more than I know about calibration and the inspection of electricity and gas, but my architect says that this is the place, not far away from the customs building, and that we need a special building for it.

Perhaps I can answer the questions one at a time. So far as distance is concerned, the building to which I refer is one block closer than the minister suggests. So far as the question of electricity and gas is concerned, there is equality. They are ^oth there. I will not quarrel with the architect, but does the architect whom the minister's department consults have charge of the building of which I am speaking?
I do not think so.

I am quite sure he does not, because if he did he would not even suggest putting up a new building if there were space available in this splendid building I speak of. It was an old store taken over at the first of the war. This government 
spent over $100,000 in renovating it and it is a good building, and if the architect has not this building in mind there is no question about disputing his judgment if he never took it into consideration in arriving at that judgment. I am not criticizing him; but I am suggesting that, this other building being there and available, and affording space, the minister might at least reconsider the matter and we might save $28,000 or $25,000, or whatever it may be.

We would not save $28,000, because we would have to renovate or refix the space for the requirements in that building which the hon. member mentions, so that there would be some expenditure. Our resident architect in every district knows about every building, belonging to the government, even though such buildings may not be under public works control. In this instance, the hon. member mentions a building which our architect has never mentioned to headquarters, and we do not even know if the building belongs to the department or is rented property, or if it is still occupied and what they intend to do about it, while the needs of weights and measures seem to be pressing enough to proceed as soon as possible with this building.
Does the minister suggest that weights and measures need any special kind of construction?

Perhaps I had better read the letter from the Department of Trade and Commerce. The garage at 529 Tenth avenue west, Calgary, in which the calibration tank is at present installed, has been sold to the Consolidated Fruit Company. The letter from the Department of Trade and Commerce states:
Oil truck calibration is particularly important in the Calgary district owing to the proximity of the Turner valley oil fields, and if we are forced out of our present quarters it will be necessary to have a new location ready so that there will be no interruption in this important public service.
I shall be pleased if you will ask your resident architect to check on this situation and make what arrangement is considered necessary. At the same time I would suggest that some consideration be given to providing a separate building which will provide calibrating space and office quarters. Tank calibration requires extra head room and only in a few buildings is this necessary height available. In Edmonton this problem was solved by putting up our own building.
The calibration can be done anywhere in the world.

Pretty easy money.

Supply-Public Works

I notice this is a revote of $25,500, which is $5,500 less than this particular vote. Does that mean that you have already started certain construction on this, and have possibly bought the site, dug the pit where your weigh scales will go, or something along that line? The actual increase is $4,000; but is the difference of $5,500 due to increased cost, or what is the explanation?

Last year we
voted $27,000. That was for 1946^7. This year we are asking for $31,000. The $25,500 is the difference between the $1,500 to pay for the site and the $27,000 we obtained last year.

That is to say, you
bought the site last year.

When these
estimates were prepared in October last year we were negotiating with the city of Calgary for the site I mentioned a moment ago, and we expected to make that payment during the fiscal year ending March this year. That payment has been made. We spent $1,452.25 on the site. This year we expect to need the difference of $25,500.

This $4,000 difference
is due to estimated increased cost of building? Mr. FOURNIER (Hull): That is right.

I come to the next
item, Calgary office building, revote of $100,000. What is that building? Where will it be erected and what is the purpose of it?

This is the note I have on the question. This is required towards the purchase of an addition to the government-owned site to provide adequate accommodation for the veterans affairs department and the unemployment insurance commission. It is proposed to erect a four-storey structure 65 feet by 200 feet, with basement and concrete foundations, masonry walls, reinforced concrete frame, brick facing, stone trim, felt and gravel roofing. It is proposed to erect the building on the government-owned site located at the north west corner of fourth street west and Sixth avenue west. This property comprises lots IS, 19 and 20 and has frontages of 130'5" on Fourth street west, and 92'9" on Sixth avenue west. The district resident architect recommends that adjoining lots, 21 and 22, located on Sixth avenue west be acquired. These lots are owned by Mrs. Marion Akins and have been valued at approximately $22,000.	,
What is the location of lots?
It is on lots 18, 19, 20, 21 and 22, northwest corner of Fourth street west and Sixth avenue west.

Before we finish with that, there is something I wish to get clear. The government-owned site which the minister speaks of at Fourth street west and Sixth avenue west is, I presume, the site upon which the courthouse is placed in Calgary and the old northwest mounted police barracks, which it has been rumoured for some time were going to be torn down. This building, I presume, is to be erected partly on the site formerly occupied by the old northwest mounted police barracks, including certain other lots there. This northwest corner of Fourth street west and Sixth avenue would be across the street from that. Do I understand that there are to be two buildings here?

It is an addition to the site or to the building we have here in Calgary. We are purchasing lots adjoining the property we now have. We are preparing or trying to prepare plans and specifications for that addition, in which to put the offices of the departments I have just named.

I do not quite understand this, because I understood the minister to say that this property would be erected at the corner of Fourth street west and Sixth avenue. As I say, that is the site of the old northwest mounted police barracks. Then they were to buy additional property on the northwest corner. But that is across the street. That is why I was wondering whether there were to be two buildings.

I will read over the description. The hon. member certainly knows more about Calgary than I do. Here is the site for this proposed new addition to the building. It is proposed to erect the building on the government-owned site located at the northwest corner of Fourth street west and Sixth avenue west. This property comprises lots 18, 19 and 20 and has frontages of so much on Fourth street west and a frontage on Sixth avenue west. The district resident architect recommends that adjoining lots 21 and 22 located on Sixth avenue west be acquired. These lots are owned by Mrs. So-and-so and are valued at so much.
I must beg the minister's pardon. I understood that the site he was talking about was the site of the old northwest mounted police barracks, but the government already owns land across the street.

Carried.

There is one other item I should like to ask about, namely "Coutts- buildings for customs and immigration (revote $126,000)." The present estimate is $140,000, an increase of $14,000. I am sorry that the money which was voted for this last year was not expended last year. I should like to assure you, Mr. Chairman, andi the committee that the customs building at Coutts is a bad advertisement for Canada. On the United States side of the border there is a good customs house and a good general set-up of government buildings which is quite impressive. The United States visitor, leaving that set-up and coming across the border into Canada at Coutts, is faced by a poor-looking old building which, I am sure, immediately gives him the impression that he is coming to a poor country which does not amount to much. Last year I was quite pleased when this vote went through for the erection of a new customs building at Coutts. When I came to Ottawa for the present session of parliament, I came by automobile and passed through Coutts on my way. I was disappointed to find that no building had taken place there during the previous summer; and the customs inspector at Coutts, to whom I spoke for some time, understood that nothing would be done until this spring at the earliest. I think the sooner the government makes use of the money which was voted for this item to erect a building on that site which will be a credit to Canada and will favourably impress people coming into this country through that port of entry, the better off we shall be. If construction has not already been started. I should like to urge strongly that it be started immediately, so that we may get reasonably well along before the present construction year has elapsed.

I understand that work is well advanced on the plans and specifications for this building. As soon as they are completed, we shall ask for tenders. We ourselves wish to proceed, because the reports we have concerning the actual buildings there indicate that they are not any credit to our country.
Definitely not.
We are doing the best we can to proceed this year.

I just understood the minister to say that they are well along with plans and specifications. But the money for this building was voted last year. Surely the plans and specifications were prepared a year ago after 
the money was voted. Surely we are not at that stage now, a year after the money for this particular building was provided for-
If the hon. member will permit me to interject, this money was voted for the first time at the end of August last year.
Yes.

I explained when my estimates first came up, on the general item, that if we had not proceeded with many of these projects it was on account of lack of staff in my office, and lack of material and man-power. I dealt with that the other day. But this is one of the most pressing projects, and we admit that. We could not complete the plans in the fiscal year ended in March this year; we are still working on them. I am informed that in the not too far distant future we shall call for tenders. Proceeding with the putting up of buildings nowadays is perhaps a little more difficult than it was in normal times before the war. I do not recall whether the hon. member was in the house on Friday and Monday night when my estimates came up.
Yes.
At that time I tried to give the committee the position of the department as to new construction.

I must say that I am very much disappointed to hear that this building, which the minister admits is a most pressing affair, has not yet had the plans and specifications for it completed. Can the minister indicate to the committee whether it will be started this year? I do not mean the plans and specifications; I mean the actual construction.

We hope to ask for tenders as soon as these plans and specifications are prepared. We will lose no time in asking for tenders, and we just express the pious hope that somebody will tender for this job.

I should like to point out that when the government really wish to get things done, it is not a matter of waiting around for people to make tenders and so forth. They get to work and get something done. The best illustration of that was what occurred in this country during the war. When we had to get things built, we got them built.
I think the same thing applies to an affair of this sort. If the government are seized of the necessity of getting a thing built, they will get it built. They will get construction started

Supply-Public Works
and do it rapidly. But as long as they are fiddling around waiting for somebody to draw up plans and specifications, and then waiting for somebody to put in a tender, I doubt whether we shall ever get the building.
Is it the suggestion of the hon. member that we go ahead and put up this building at all costs?

The suggestion I am making is that the Department of Public Works should, in carrying out their duties, show that degree of energy which a department of this dominion should show, instead of playing around with the job.

I do not often play around with a job. Some months from now, when the hon. member comes to read over what he has just said about the procedure the Department of Public Works should follow, I think he may be sorry for suggesting that method of procedure. In our department since confederation we have established some rules of procedure for the protection of public money, and the best way which has been devised, under every government, has been to prepare plans and specifications, call for tenders, and give contracts to the lowest bidders. If the hon. member thinks that in normal times we should return to the procedure we followed in war time-well, if that were done I do not know whether the government to which I belong would wish to occupy these benches. You cannot run this department by trying to have work done at all costs. You have to get the best for the money the people are paying into the coffers of the country. I know of no other way of doing the work.

I was not suggesting that this should be done at all costs. I was suggesting that a sufficient amount of energy should be put behind it to get it done. To my knowledge, this thing has been projected at least since 1938, and it may have been projected for many years before that. It is now nine years later; and I realize, of course, that a war has intervened. But surely when the thing was projected as long as nine years ago the government would have plans and specifications, so that when parliament voted money last year they could go ahead with it; that is, if they had enough energy, initiative and good organization to run the public works of this country in a way which, in my opinion, they should be run.
Mr. FOURNIER (Hull); That is a matter of opinion. Let me tell the hon. member that in the last five years I have been head of the
department the hon. member is the first one who has told me that my officials lack energy and foresight and that they have not done their work. I would call as witness nearly every member sitting opposite. They will * say that in my department they receive courteous attention and service and have had results when they have made requests. When the hon. member expresses his opinion about the running of the Department of Public Works I feel just a little sorry for those old servants we have had for many years in the department who do their utmost at all times.
In connection with what the minister has said-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, The hon. member for Red Deer has been endeavouring for the last fifteen minutes to speak. I do not want to cut off the discussion between the minister and the hon. member for Calgary East too abruptly, but in fairness to other hon. members I must say I believe they should be given an opportunity.

The only redeeming feature about getting up and down so often is that I secure exercise which I might not otherwise get. I appreciate very much, Mr. Chairman, your having recognized the fact that I have made an effort to get to my feet.
Speaking about public buildings and proposed construction when the general item was before the committee on June 20, the minister indicated that a great many projects had been urged upon him, and he also analysed certain problems confronting his department in this regard. I fully appreciate the problem with which the minister is confronted. However, as he is probably aware, conditions vary somewhat from area to area so far as available labour is concerned, and I believe that is also true with respect to materials.
So far as I can learn from a return brought down, the minister's supplementary estimates last year included a sum of $107,000 for the public work at Red Deer. That was later deleted, and I believe I appreciate the reason for that being done. The situation there is serious. I believe the Post Office Department has been successful in impressing upon the Minister of Public Works the urgent necessity of undertaking that project at the earliest possible moment. I find in the return that the deputy minister of public works did indicate to the deputy postmaster general that the item had been included last year but was subsequently deleted. He pointed out, however, that it would be given further consideration this year.
I am not going to take more time on the matter. If I were to try I believe I could
Supply-Public Works

paint a dismal picture respecting the situation there. I would urge upon the minister that, if at all possible, the appropriation be given favourable consideration this year and that steps be taken toward completion of the project. I believe it stands pretty much by itself as one of the most serious in Canada today.	,
Has the minister received any request from the people at Fairview in the Peace River district for a new post office building?

I have probably received it, although I have not the communication with me. But, speaking generally, and also replying to the hon. member who has just spoken, may I point out that I believe there are three or four hundred requests for buildings throughout the country by different departments of government. Those buildings are held up because we and our advisers are convinced that we cannot proceed with them. There is no bad will about the matter, nor is there any discrimination. We are a service department, and we follow the recommendations and requests of all the other departments.
All hon. members could, I have no doubt, describe pitiful cases respecting space in their respective constituencies or towns. The minister himself is in the same position with respect to some public buildings. The work has been delayed because we know we shall not be able to proceed this year with those projects, and we do not feel we should have amounts put into the estimates uselessly.
Last year we did try that procedure, and I must admit that a large number of the votes this year are revotes of last year which could not be expended. Why should we pad the estimates this year when I know, and those who advise me know that we shall not expend the money or succeed in putting up those ouildings?
Just to see, for myself, last year I travelled this country from one end to the other, not because I did not rely upon the reports I had received from officials in my department in the different districts, but so that I could meet other people and see conditions. I do not mean that in one place we could not put up a building; but, as a general policy, we cannot proceed. With materials and labour available, it would be only proper that they should be directed to the construction of houses. Not more than three weeks ago I had a conference to see if we could, during the fall, proceed with some new works, but I am told that it still would not be feasible.

I ask particularly about Fair-view because it is a fast-growing town in one

of the best farming districts in western Canada. It is going to be thickly populated1, and at the present time the post office is housed in the back part of an old and dilapidated rough-board building, with floors which have become so uneven because of the seepage of water that people can scarcely walk across them without tripping. The space in which to handle mail is most inadequate. The roof is leaking to a point *where I am satisfied the mails are endangered. I must point out the total inadequacy of the building to handle the work of the Post Office Department.
Just by way of contrast, let me say that in the town of Peace River is a first-class building. Let me congratulate the minister and his department upon maintaining at that point one of the finest public buildings I have seen in any western Canadian town. Not only is it well built, but it is extremely well looked after. It has the most up-to-date equipment, which is a splendid thing. I should like to impress upon the minister that if he cannot see his way clear to build a small well-equipped building in Fairview, he and his officials do something about renting some other place at which a post office could be located.

Or repair the
present building?

That is the
amount required to pay the government's portion of sewer and water services for the post office and telegraph buildings, alterations to the post office drain and the installation of plumbing in the telegraph building.

I wanted to make it quite
clear when I spoke that I appreciate fully the problems confronting the minister, but I am concerned over this item having been included in the supplementary estimates and then deleted before they were presented to the house.

A request will
come to the Department of Public Works from the Post Office Department. We prepare either the main or supplementary estimates which go before treasury board and then before the government. The mere fact that a department recommends an expenditure does not mean that it will go through. These items are studied and brought before treasury board and government where the final decision is made.

I just want to emphasize
that the urgency of this project was recognized

Supply-Public Works
and I hope it will not be relegated to the bottom of the ladder when the time comes that the department can undertake these projects. As I say, both the Post Office Department and the Department of Public Works have recognized the urgency of this.

I want to be
fair. If it is a new building I cannot commit myself. I made the same answer to the hon. member's colleagues on the other side.

I am simply asking that at
some future time when conditions permit the construction of new buildings, this project, the importance of which has been recognized, be not relegated to a position at the bottom of the construction ladder. I hope it will be one of the first undertaken because the condition is quite serious. I am not asking for special consideration at the moment.

I wonder if I might have the indulgence of the committee to ask a simple, non-controversial question on item 290. I should like to ask if there is any provision in the vote for $75,000 for an addition to the post office in Swift Current?

This vote is
required for improvements and repairs in connection with dominion public buildings in Saskatchewan. It is not known in advance what repairs will be required. If Swift Current is in need of repairs I am sure the architect will make a report and the repairs will be made.

With reference to the item, William Head quarantine station, alterations, improvements and repairs, $66,000 there is, as an adjunct of that quarantine station, a leper station on Bentinck island. Could the minister say whether any proportion of this $66,000 is to be spent on alterations, improvements and repairs to the buildings and establishments on that island?

A contract was let for repairs to the different buildings. An order in council was passed, April 24, 1947, granting authority to accept the tender of Canada Paint and Contracting Company at $66,894 for general repairs, painting, plumbing and heating installations at the quarantine station at William Head. Two bids were received, one from H. V. Jones at $69,628.27, and one from Canada Paint and Contracting Company at $66,984.
Among the works at Bentinck island are patients' cabins Nos. 1, 2 3, 4 and 5 and meat house No. 9, repairs and improvements, $3,350; nurses' residence, painting, improve-

ments to heating and repairs, $985; attendants' residence, improvements to plumbing, repairs and painting, $1,240.

I suggest that, since there are only three patients there and since there have only been from two to three patients in that station in the last ten years, that is a very large amount of money to spend on such an establishment. There is another leper station in eastern Canada at Tracadie, where there are only seven lepers, and since the general maintenance of the leper station at William Head costs some $5,000 a year I suggest that this expenditure seems a lot for just three men. One is a Chinaman, one a Jap, and one is a white missionary who has just been sent there. If we are to spend money there it might be advisable to send the seven patients from eastern Canada out there, or if you are not going to do that, would it not be wise to move the three from this island and send them to Tracadie? But an expenditure such as is suggested is a lot of money to spend to look after three men.

I agree. But the hon. member understands that these repairs are being made at the request of the Department of National Health and Welfare. All we do is act as agents for the department. I think the remarks made by the hon. gentleman are very sensible. There are, I understand, only two of these leper stations in Canada, one in New Brunswick and the other on Bentinck island. Perhaps they could send these three patients on Bentinck island to the other leper station at Tracadie, where there are more than three patients.

I do not mind whether you transfer the three to New Brunswick or transfer the seven to western Canada, but it does seem unnecessary to go ahead and spend this money for just three patients. I would suggest that the minister refer the matter back to the Department of National Health and Welfare.

I should like to direct one inquiry to the Minister of Public Works. He spoke about the red ensign. I take it that is the same flag which the hon. member for Royal rightly described as the Canadian ensign.

The Canadian ensign.
The mutilated coat of arms.

I understand that in my riding some officials in dominion buildings have had a letter from some department of government advising them that only the Canadian red ensign was to be flown from a dominion public building in that town. Is it true that an official letter has been sent out? Did the department send it out? Under whose direction was it sent out?

This is the policy of the government concerning the flying of the flag. The position of my officials was that they had an order in council which was passed in 1945 on the flying of the red ensign. The policy is as follows:
The flying of the red ensign as a flag distinctive of Canada, was authorized by an order in council P.C. 5888 on September 5, 1945. The red ensign has been flying on the parliament buildings since that date, and the Department of Public Works has gradually been substituting the red ensign for the union jack on public buildings as the supply of union jacks becomes exhausted, and the supply of red1 ensigns becomes available. This policy is in line with the decision made by parliament when a committee of both houses was set up in the first session of the present parliament.
During the duration of world war I by the order of the deputy minister dated 4th September, 1917, the flags were flown every day of the year from all public buildings in the dominion.
. After the conclusion of the war the continuation of this policy of flying the flags daily was 
taken up with the hon. the minister, dated the 18th July, 1919. The flags were ordered to be flown every day throughout the year.
This is the policy which guides the officials of my department.
The minister just made the statement that it was left to some official in the public building which flag was to be chosen to fly.
Do not mistake what I said. When an official who flies the flag on a building where he is an official, asks the department for a union jack-
He gets it?
I do not know of a case where it has been refused. If they want the other one they receive it. I do not know if I can do anything better than that.
I am just trying to find out which is correct?
Which is which?

Did the hon. member see the letter? We gave no instructions to force them to fly one flag or the other. I have read exactly what has taken place, and I want this on the record so that there will be no misunderstanding. I have read the policy to the committee. If the hon. member wishes to have one flag on the building in his home town and we receive that request they receive the flag they ask for. I am told that is what has been done by the officials.
I am wondering who has the right to decide.
